<pasted_content id="cc99">
# Take-home test: Kitchen Display Queue

## 1) What this is

Build a small internal tool for a restaurant kitchen. The expeditor (the person who decides what the kitchen works on next) needs a screen that shows every active order ranked by priority, and lets them move each order through its preparation stages.

This exercise is intentionally small. We expect you to use an AI assistant (Cursor, Claude, or similar). We are not grading how much code you can produce. We are grading whether the result is well-organized, whether the business rules live in the right layer, and whether you can explain the decisions you made.

In the technical panel you will walk us through your decisions, and you will change the running code in response to a product request we have not shared here. Design the project so that a change to ranking or to status rules is local and quick.

**Time box:** 4 hours, stop when you hit it. A smaller result with an honest decision log is a better submission than a wide one you cannot explain.

## 2) AI

You may use any AI tool for any part of this exercise.

You must be able to explain every file you submit, including code you did not type yourself. During the panel we will open specific functions and ask why they are written that way. A file you cannot explain works against you.

In `DECISIONS.md`, name one AI suggestion you kept and one you rejected or rewrote. Be specific: quote the idea, not the tool brand.

Include your AI chat logs in the repository. Create a folder called `ai-logs/` at the root and export the full conversation history from the tool you used (screenshots, markdown exports, or .json files — whatever your tool supports). We will not penalize you for wrong turns or failed attempts in the logs; we want to see how you steered the tool, what you asked, and when you course-corrected.

## 3) Domain

A restaurant receives orders throughout the day. Each order has a type (dine-in, takeout, or delivery), a list of menu items, and optionally a promised time. The kitchen does not prepare orders in arrival order; instead, a priority score determines the queue. The expeditor uses this screen to see what to work on next and to advance each order through its stages.

No authentication, no payments, no real customer data.

## 4) Data Model

### 4.1) Menu item (provided by seed, no CRUD needed)

| FIELD | RULES |
|---|---|
| `name` | Unique, non-empty |
| `category` | `starter`, `main_course`, `dessert`, or `drink` |
| `prep_time_minutes` | Integer > 0 |

### 4.2) Order

| FIELD | RULES |
|---|---|
| `customer_name` | Non-empty string |
| `type` | `dine_in`, `takeout`, or `delivery` |
| `placed_at` | Timestamp, set on creation |
| `promised_at` | Timestamp or null. Relevant for `delivery` and `takeout`. |
| `is_vip` | Boolean |
| `status` | `received`, `preparing`, `ready`, `picked_up`, or `cancelled` |

### 4.3) Order item (join table)

| FIELD | RULES |
|---|---|
| `order_id` | References an existing Order |
| `menu_item_id` | References an existing Menu Item |
| `quantity` | Integer > 0 |

## 5) Priority Queue

The default queue lists orders in `received` or `preparing` status. Terminal orders (`picked_up`, `cancelled`) and `ready` orders stay out of the active queue.

Sort by priority score, highest first. The score is computed at request time, using the real clock in the running app and a frozen `now` in tests. All time comparisons use UTC.

### 5.1) Score

| INPUT | | POINTS |
|---|---|---|
| Order type | `dine_in` | 30 |
| | `takeout` | 20 |
| | `delivery` | 10 |
| VIP | +20 if `is_vip` is true | |
| Wait time | `min(40, floor(minutes_waiting / 10) * 5)` | |
| Promised time | `promised_at` is within 30 minutes from now | 25 |
| | `promised_at` is within 31–60 minutes from now | 15 |
| | `promised_at` is more than 60 minutes away or null | 0 |
| Complexity | `min(20, floor(total_prep_minutes / 15) * 5)` | |

Where:

- `minutes_waiting` = whole minutes elapsed since `placed_at`, floored. An order placed 9 minutes and 50 seconds ago has 9 whole minutes = 0 wait-time points;
- `total_prep_minutes` = sum of (`prep_time_minutes * quantity`) across all items in the order;

### 5.2) Tie-break

When two orders have the same score, sort by:

1. Earlier `promised_at` first (`null` goes last);
2. Earlier `placed_at` first;
3. Smaller `id` first;

### 5.3) Worked Examples

All examples use `now = 2026-06-15T12:00:00Z`.

#### Example A

A `dine_in` order, not VIP, placed at `2026-06-15T11:25:00Z` (35 minutes ago), no `promised_at`. The order has 2x Grilled Salmon (prep_time 20 min) and 1x Caesar Salad (prep_time 10 min). Total prep = (20 * 2) + (10 * 1) = 50 minutes.

| COMPONENT | CALCULATION | POINTS |
|---|---|---|
| Type | `dine_in` | 30 |
| VIP | not VIP | 0 |
| Wait time | `min(40, floor(35 / 10) * 5) = min(40, 15)` | 15 |
| Promised | null | 0 |
| Complexity | `min(20, floor(50 / 15) * 5) = min(20, 15)` | 15 |
| **Total** | | **60** |

#### Example B

A `delivery` order, VIP, placed at `2026-06-15T11:50:00Z` (10 minutes ago), `promised_at = 2026-06-15T12:20:00Z` (20 minutes from now). The order has 1x Margherita Pizza (prep_time 12 min). Total prep = 12 minutes.

| COMPONENT | CALCULATION | POINTS |
|---|---|---|
| Type | `delivery` | 10 |
| VIP | VIP | 20 |
| Wait time | `min(40, floor(10 / 10) * 5) = min(40, 5)` | 5 |
| Promised | 20 min from now (within 30) | 25 |
| Complexity | `min(20, floor(12 / 15) * 5) = min(20, 0)` | 0 |
| **Total** | | **60** |

Both score 60. Tie-break: Example B has a `promised_at` and A does not, so B ranks above A.

## 6) Status changes (state machine)

| FROM | TO | RULE |
|---|---|---|
| `received` | `preparing` | Allowed |
| `received` | `cancelled` | Allowed |
| `preparing` | `ready` | Allowed |
| `ready` | `picked_up` | Allowed |
| anything else | anything else | Rejected |

`picked_up` and `cancelled` are terminal. No order can skip a step (`received` cannot jump to `ready`). Repeating the same transition (e.g. acknowledging an already `preparing` order) is an error, not a silent success.

Enforce this on the server, hiding a button in the UI is not enough. If someone calls the API directly, the server must reject an illegal transition with a clear error.

## 7) API

| METHOD | PATH | BEHAVIOR |
|---|---|---|
| GET | `/orders/queue` | Default: `received` and `preparing`, sorted by score. Optional query param `status=received` or `status=preparing` to filter. Each order in the response includes its computed `score`. |
| POST | `/orders/:id/start` | Transition: `received → preparing`. |
| POST | `/orders/:id/ready` | Transition: `preparing → ready`. |
| POST | `/orders/:id/pickup` | Transition: `ready → picked_up`. |
| POST | `/orders/:id/cancel` | Transition: `received → cancelled`. |

For illegal transitions or other validation errors, return a 4xx response with a stable, machine-readable error code (e.g. `INVALID_TRANSITION`, `ORDER_NOT_FOUND`). Choose your codes and document them briefly in the README.

## 8) UI

One page: the Kitchen Display.

- A table showing the active queue: score, customer name, order type, items summary, wait time, promised time, VIP badge, status;
- A way to filter by `received`, `preparing`, or the default active queue;
- Actions to advance each order to its next status. Only show the action that is valid for the current status;
- A way to cancel a `received` order;
- An empty state when the queue has no orders;
- When the API rejects a transition, the error must be visible on the screen (not just in the browser console);

Use MUI. Match the layout to a dense internal tool (think ops dashboard), not a marketing page.

The score and the sort order must come from the API. The UI must not contain a second copy of the scoring formula. The table displays whatever the API returns, in the order the API returns it.

## 9) Technical constraints

One repository, wwo apps (API and web). Do not depend on any private or external repository.

### 9.1) API

- Node.js 22;
- JavaScript;
- Express;
- Sequelize 6, with migrations (do not rely on `sync()` for schema creation);
- PostgreSQL 16;
- Jest;

Organize the API in layers:

| LAYER | RESPONSIBILITY |
|---|---|
| Endpoint | HTTP only. Read the request, call the module, write the response. Thin. |
| Module | Business logic: priority scoring, state machine transitions. |
| Repository | Data access: Sequelize queries, includes, filters. |
| Schema | Sequelize models and migrations. |

The priority function must be pure. It receives the order data and `now` as arguments, and returns a number. Its Jest tests run without PostgreSQL and without mocking Sequelize.

### 9.2) Web

- Vite;
- React 19;
- TypeScript;
- MUI 7;
- Vitest (for extra points only; see below);

### 9.3) Database

Ship a `docker-compose.yml` that starts PostgreSQL 16 only. Use host port `5433` so a local Postgres on `5432` does not collide.

```yaml
services:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: kitchen_queue
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: kitchen_queue
      POSTGRES_DB: kitchen_queue
    ports:
      - "5433:5432"
```

### 9.4) Getting started

From a clean machine, the README should guide someone through:

1. `docker compose up -d` (start Postgres)
2. One install command
3. One `db:setup` command (runs migrations + seed)
4. One dev command (starts both the API and the web app)

Suggested ports: API on `4000`, web on `5173`.

### 9.5) Seed

You write the seed, it must contain menu items and orders with order items.

Seed dates must be relative to the UTC time when the seed runs (e.g. "placed 2 hours ago", "promised in 20 minutes"). Hard-coded calendar dates go stale and break the demo.

Include enough rows to demonstrate:

- Every order type (`dine_in`, `takeout`, `delivery`)
- At least one VIP and one non-VIP order
- A wait-time cap (an order old enough that wait-time points hit the maximum)
- A complexity cap (an order with enough total prep time to hit the maximum)
- A tie on score broken by `promised_at`
- Orders in different statuses (`received`, `preparing`, and at least one `ready` that is not in the active queue)

Tests do not use the seed, they pass their own fixtures and a frozen `now`.

## 10) Tests (Required)

| FRAMEWORK | WHAT IS PROVES |
|---|---|
| Jest (priority) | Score calculation, both caps (wait-time and complexity), all `promised_at` buckets (within 30 min, within 60 min, beyond, null), tie-break, and at least one case where a lower base-weight type wins on the rest of the formula (e.g. a delivery VIP with a tight promise beats a dine_in non-VIP). |
| Jest (transitions) | Every legal transition succeeds. Illegal transitions are rejected (skipping a step, repeating the same status, transitioning from a terminal status). A cancelled or picked-up order does not appear in the default queue. |

Priority tests must freeze `now`. A test that calls `Date.now()` and hopes the clock still matches is a failing submission.

## 11) Extra points

Do these only after the required core is solid and you can fully explain it. Skipping all of them does not count against you. In `DECISIONS.md`, note which extras you attempted and which you left out.

### 11.1) POST /orders endpoint

API only, no UI form needed. Validate that `items` is non-empty, each `menu_item_id` references an existing menu item, and each `quantity` is a positive integer. Include at least one Jest test for a validation error.

### 11.2) Vitest component test

The cancel button is only shown for `received` orders; or the queue table renders an empty state when there are no orders.

### 11.3) Playwright end-to-end

One happy path: the queue renders a seeded order, the expeditor starts preparation, and the status changes on screen. Wire it with Playwright's `webServer` config so `npm run test:e2e` boots what it needs.

## 12) What to submit

A git repository we can clone, with:

- `README.md` — prerequisites (Docker, Node 22), the four commands to get running, ports, and your API error codes;
- `DECISIONS.md` — the sections listed below;
- The API, the web app, migrations, seed, and tests;

### 12.1) DECISIONS.md sections

Write a few short paragraphs for each. We read these before the panel.

1. **Scope**
   - What you built and what you cut because of the 4-hour box. Which extra points you attempted and which you skipped;
2. **Layers**
   - What lives in the module, the repository, and the UI. Name one rule you refused to put in the UI and why;
3. **Priority**
   - How the score is produced at request time, and one edge case that was easy to get wrong;
4. **Transitions**
   - Where the state machine is enforced, and what happens when someone tries to start an order that is already `preparing`;
5. **AI**
   - One AI suggestion you kept and one you rejected or rewrote. Quote the idea and explain your reasoning;
6. **Next**
   - If this had to run in a real kitchen next month, name the first two changes you would make. Do not implement them;

## 13) The Interview

Plan on a short walkthrough of your `DECISIONS.md` and the priority rule, followed by a live change to this repository. The change will be a product tweak to ranking or status, in the area you already built. We will not ask you to re-architect the app, and we will not ask you to implement the extra-point items.

## 3) Domain

A restaurant receives orders throughout the day. Each order has a type (dine-in, takeout, or delivery), a list of menu items, and optionally a promised time. The kitchen does not prepare orders in arrival order; instead, a priority score determines the queue. The expeditor uses this screen to see what to work on next and to advance each order through its stages.

No authentication, no payments, no real customer data.

## 4) Data Model

### 4.1) Menu item (provided by seed, no CRUD needed)

| FIELD | RULES |
|---|---|
| `name` | Unique, non-empty |
| `category` | `starter`, `main_course`, `dessert`, or `drink` |
| `prep_time_minutes` | Integer > 0 |

### 4.2) Order

| FIELD | RULES |
|---|---|
| `customer_name` | Non-empty string |
| `type` | `dine_in`, `takeout`, or `delivery` |
| `placed_at` | Timestamp, set on creation |
| `promised_at` | Timestamp or null. Relevant for `delivery` and `takeout`. |
| `is_vip` | Boolean |
| `status` | `received`, `preparing`, `ready`, `picked_up`, or `cancelled` |

### 4.3) Order item (join table)

| FIELD | RULES |
|---|---|
| `order_id` | References an existing Order |
| `menu_item_id` | References an existing Menu Item |
| `quantity` | Integer > 0 |

## 5) Priority Queue

The default queue lists orders in `received` or `preparing` status. Terminal orders (`picked_up`, `cancelled`) and `ready` orders stay out of the active queue.

Sort by priority score, highest first. The score is computed at request time, using the real clock in the running app and a frozen `now` in tests. All time comparisons use UTC.

### 5.1) Score

| INPUT | | POINTS |
|---|---|---|
| Order type | `dine_in` | 30 |
| | `takeout` | 20 |
| | `delivery` | 10 |
| VIP | +20 if `is_vip` is true | |
| Wait time | `min(40, floor(minutes_waiting / 10) * 5)` | |
| Promised time | `promised_at` is within 30 minutes from now | 25 |
| | `promised_at` is within 31–60 minutes from now | 15 |
| | `promised_at` is more than 60 minutes away or null | 0 |
| Complexity | `min(20, floor(total_prep_minutes / 15) * 5)` | |

Where:

- `minutes_waiting` = whole minutes elapsed since `placed_at`, floored. An order placed 9 minutes and 50 seconds ago has 9 whole minutes = 0 wait-time points;
- `total_prep_minutes` = sum of (`prep_time_minutes * quantity`) across all items in the order;

### 5.2) Tie-break

When two orders have the same score, sort by:

1. Earlier `promised_at` first (`null` goes last);
2. Earlier `placed_at` first;
3. Smaller `id` first;

A `dine_in` order, not VIP, placed at `2026-06-15T11:25:00Z` (35 minutes ago), no `promised_at`. The order has 2x Grilled Salmon (prep_time 20 min) and 1x Caesar Salad (prep_time 10 min). Total prep = (20 * 2) + (10 * 1) = 50 minutes.

| COMPONENT | CALCULATION | POINTS |
|---|---|---|
| Type | `dine_in` | 30 |
| VIP | not VIP | 0 |
| Wait time | `min(40, floor(35 / 10) * 5) = min(40, 15)` | 15 |
| Promised | null | 0 |
| Complexity | `min(20, floor(50 / 15) * 5) = min(20, 15)` | 15 |
| **Total** | | **60** |

#### Example B

A `delivery` order, VIP, placed at `2026-06-15T11:50:00Z` (10 minutes ago), `promised_at = 2026-06-15T12:20:00Z` (20 minutes from now). The order has 1x Margherita Pizza (prep_time 12 min). Total prep = 12 minutes.

| COMPONENT | CALCULATION | POINTS |
|---|---|---|
| Type | `delivery` | 10 |
| VIP | VIP | 20 |
| Wait time | `min(40, floor(10 / 10) * 5) = min(40, 5)` | 5 |
| Promised | 20 min from now (within 30) | 25 |
| Complexity | `min(20, floor(12 / 15) * 5) = min(20, 0)` | 0 |
| **Total** | | **60** |

| FROM | TO | RULE |
|---|---|---|
| `received` | `preparing` | Allowed |
| `received` | `cancelled` | Allowed |
| `preparing` | `ready` | Allowed |
| `ready` | `picked_up` | Allowed |
| anything else | anything else | Rejected |

One repository, wwo apps (API and web). Do not depend on any private or external repository.

- Node.js 22;
- JavaScript;
- Express;

- PostgreSQL 16;
- Jest;

| LAYER | RESPONSIBILITY |
|---|---|

| Module | Business logic: priority scoring, state machine transitions. |
| Repository | Data access: Sequelize queries, includes, filters. |
| Schema | Sequelize models and migrations. |

The priority function must be pure. It receives the order data and `now` as arguments, and returns a number. Its Jest tests run without PostgreSQL and without mocking Sequelize.

- Vite;
- React 19;
- TypeScript;
- MUI 7;
- Vitest (for extra points only; see below);

4. One dev command (starts both the API and the web app)

# Take-home test: Kitchen Display Queue

> Verbatim copy of the original assignment. Source of truth. Do not edit.

## 1) What this is

Build a small internal tool for a restaurant kitchen. The expeditor (the person who decides what the kitchen works on next) needs a screen that shows every active order ranked by priority, and lets them move each order through its preparation stages.

This exercise is intentionally small. We expect you to use an AI assistant (Cursor, Claude, or similar). We are not grading how much code you can produce. We are grading whether the result is well-organized, whether the business rules live in the right layer, and whether you can explain the decisions you made.

In the technical panel you will walk us through your decisions, and you will change the running code in response to a product request we have not shared here. Design the project so that a change to ranking or to status rules is local and quick.

**Time box:** 4 hours, stop when you hit it. A smaller result with an honest decision log is a better submission than a wide one you cannot explain.

## 2) AI

You may use any AI tool for any part of this exercise.

You must be able to explain every file you submit, including code you did not type yourself. During the panel we will open specific functions and ask why they are written that way. A file you cannot explain works against you.

In `DECISIONS.md`, name one AI suggestion you kept and one you rejected or rewrote. Be specific: quote the idea, not the tool brand.

Include your AI chat logs in the repository. Create a folder called `ai-logs/` at the root and export the full conversation history from the tool you used (screenshots, markdown exports, or .json files — whatever your tool supports). We will not penalize you for wrong turns or failed attempts in the logs; we want to see how you steered the tool, what you asked, and when you course-corrected.

## 3) Domain

A restaurant receives orders throughout the day. Each order has a type (dine-in, takeout, or delivery), a list of menu items, and optionally a promised time. The kitchen does not prepare orders in arrival order; instead, a priority score determines the queue. The expeditor uses this screen to see what to work on next and to advance each order through its stages.

No authentication, no payments, no real customer data.

## 4) Data Model

### 4.1) Menu item (provided by seed, no CRUD needed)

| FIELD | RULES |
|---|---|
| `name` | Unique, non-empty |
| `category` | `starter`, `main_course`, `dessert`, or `drink` |
| `prep_time_minutes` | Integer > 0 |

### 4.2) Order

| FIELD | RULES |
|---|---|
| `customer_name` | Non-empty string |
| `type` | `dine_in`, `takeout`, or `delivery` |
| `placed_at` | Timestamp, set on creation |
| `promised_at` | Timestamp or null. Relevant for `delivery` and `takeout`. |
| `is_vip` | Boolean |
| `status` | `received`, `preparing`, `ready`, `picked_up`, or `cancelled` |

### 4.3) Order item (join table)

| FIELD | RULES |
|---|---|
| `order_id` | References an existing Order |
| `menu_item_id` | References an existing Menu Item |
| `quantity` | Integer > 0 |

## 5) Priority Queue

The default queue lists orders in `received` or `preparing` status. Terminal orders (`picked_up`, `cancelled`) and `ready` orders stay out of the active queue.

Sort by priority score, highest first. The score is computed at request time, using the real clock in the running app and a frozen `now` in tests. All time comparisons use UTC.

### 5.1) Score

| INPUT | | POINTS |
|---|---|---|
| Order type | `dine_in` | 30 |
| | `takeout` | 20 |
| | `delivery` | 10 |
| VIP | +20 if `is_vip` is true | |
| Wait time | `min(40, floor(minutes_waiting / 10) * 5)` | |
| Promised time | `promised_at` is within 30 minutes from now | 25 |
| | `promised_at` is within 31–60 minutes from now | 15 |
| | `promised_at` is more than 60 minutes away or null | 0 |
| Complexity | `min(20, floor(total_prep_minutes / 15) * 5)` | |

Where:

- `minutes_waiting` = whole minutes elapsed since `placed_at`, floored. An order placed 9 minutes and 50 seconds ago has 9 whole minutes = 0 wait-time points;
- `total_prep_minutes` = sum of (`prep_time_minutes * quantity`) across all items in the order;

### 5.2) Tie-break

When two orders have the same score, sort by:

1. Earlier `promised_at` first (`null` goes last);
2. Earlier `placed_at` first;
3. Smaller `id` first;

### 5.3) Worked Examples

All examples use `now = 2026-06-15T12:00:00Z`.

#### Example A

A `dine_in` order, not VIP, placed at `2026-06-15T11:25:00Z` (35 minutes ago), no `promised_at`. The order has 2x Grilled Salmon (prep_time 20 min) and 1x Caesar Salad (prep_time 10 min). Total prep = (20 * 2) + (10 * 1) = 50 minutes.

| COMPONENT | CALCULATION | POINTS |
|---|---|---|
| Type | `dine_in` | 30 |
| VIP | not VIP | 0 |
| Wait time | `min(40, floor(35 / 10) * 5) = min(40, 15)` | 15 |
| Promised | null | 0 |
| Complexity | `min(20, floor(50 / 15) * 5) = min(20, 15)` | 15 |
| **Total** | | **60** |

#### Example B

A `delivery` order, VIP, placed at `2026-06-15T11:50:00Z` (10 minutes ago), `promised_at = 2026-06-15T12:20:00Z` (20 minutes from now). The order has 1x Margherita Pizza (prep_time 12 min). Total prep = 12 minutes.

| COMPONENT | CALCULATION | POINTS |
|---|---|---|
| Type | `delivery` | 10 |
| VIP | VIP | 20 |
| Wait time | `min(40, floor(10 / 10) * 5) = min(40, 5)` | 5 |
| Promised | 20 min from now (within 30) | 25 |
| Complexity | `min(20, floor(12 / 15) * 5) = min(20, 0)` | 0 |
| **Total** | | **60** |

Both score 60. Tie-break: Example B has a `promised_at` and A does not, so B ranks above A.

## 6) Status changes (state machine)

| FROM | TO | RULE |
|---|---|---|
| `received` | `preparing` | Allowed |
| `received` | `cancelled` | Allowed |
| `preparing` | `ready` | Allowed |
| `ready` | `picked_up` | Allowed |
| anything else | anything else | Rejected |

`picked_up` and `cancelled` are terminal. No order can skip a step (`received` cannot jump to `ready`). Repeating the same transition (e.g. acknowledging an already `preparing` order) is an error, not a silent success.

Enforce this on the server, hiding a button in the UI is not enough. If someone calls the API directly, the server must reject an illegal transition with a clear error.

## 7) API

| METHOD | PATH | BEHAVIOR |
|---|---|---|
| GET | `/orders/queue` | Default: `received` and `preparing`, sorted by score. Optional query param `status=received` or `status=preparing` to filter. Each order in the response includes its computed `score`. |
| POST | `/orders/:id/start` | Transition: `received → preparing`. |
| POST | `/orders/:id/ready` | Transition: `preparing → ready`. |
| POST | `/orders/:id/pickup` | Transition: `ready → picked_up`. |
| POST | `/orders/:id/cancel` | Transition: `received → cancelled`. |

For illegal transitions or other validation errors, return a 4xx response with a stable, machine-readable error code (e.g. `INVALID_TRANSITION`, `ORDER_NOT_FOUND`). Choose your codes and document them briefly in the README.

## 8) UI

One page: the Kitchen Display.

- A table showing the active queue: score, customer name, order type, items summary, wait time, promised time, VIP badge, status;
- A way to filter by `received`, `preparing`, or the default active queue;
- Actions to advance each order to its next status. Only show the action that is valid for the current status;
- A way to cancel a `received` order;
- An empty state when the queue has no orders;
- When the API rejects a transition, the error must be visible on the screen (not just in the browser console);

Use MUI. Match the layout to a dense internal tool (think ops dashboard), not a marketing page.

The score and the sort order must come from the API. The UI must not contain a second copy of the scoring formula. The table displays whatever the API returns, in the order the API returns it.

## 9) Technical constraints

One repository, wwo apps (API and web). Do not depend on any private or external repository.

### 9.1) API

- Node.js 22;
- JavaScript;
- Express;
- Sequelize 6, with migrations (do not rely on `sync()` for schema creation);
- PostgreSQL 16;
- Jest;

Organize the API in layers:

| LAYER | RESPONSIBILITY |
|---|---|
| Endpoint | HTTP only. Read the request, call the module, write the response. Thin. |
| Module | Business logic: priority scoring, state machine transitions. |
| Repository | Data access: Sequelize queries, includes, filters. |
| Schema | Sequelize models and migrations. |

The priority function must be pure. It receives the order data and `now` as arguments, and returns a number. Its Jest tests run without PostgreSQL and without mocking Sequelize.

### 9.2) Web

- Vite;
- React 19;
- TypeScript;
- MUI 7;
- Vitest (for extra points only; see below);

### 9.3) Database

Ship a `docker-compose.yml` that starts PostgreSQL 16 only. Use host port `5433` so a local Postgres on `5432` does not collide.

```yaml
services:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: kitchen_queue
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: kitchen_queue
      POSTGRES_DB: kitchen_queue
    ports:
      - "5433:5432"
```

### 9.4) Getting started

From a clean machine, the README should guide someone through:

1. `docker compose up -d` (start Postgres)
2. One install command
3. One `db:setup` command (runs migrations + seed)
4. One dev command (starts both the API and the web app)

Vou explicar com calma. E sim: Express, Sequelize e as outras ferramentas **são exigências do teste**, não escolha minha. Estão na seção 9 ("Technical constraints").

## O que é a atividade

Imagine a cozinha de um restaurante. Chegam pedidos o dia todo, e alguém, o **expeditor** (uma espécie de coordenador da cozinha), decide qual pedido a cozinha faz primeiro.

Ele não segue a ordem de chegada. Cada pedido ganha uma **nota de prioridade** (o "score"), e quem tem a nota maior vai para o topo da fila.

Você precisa construir:
1. **Uma tela** com a lista de pedidos ordenada por essa nota.
2. **Botões** para mudar o status de cada pedido: "comecei a preparar", "ficou pronto", "foi retirado" ou "cancelar".

## Como a nota é calculada

A nota é a soma de cinco partes:

| Parte | Regra |
|---|---|
| Tipo do pedido | comer no local = 30, retirada = 20, entrega = 10 |
| Cliente VIP | +20 |
| Tempo esperando | +5 a cada 10 minutos, no máximo 40 |
| Horário prometido | prometido para daqui a até 30 min = 25; de 31 a 60 min = 15; mais longe ou sem horário = 0 |
| Complexidade | +5 a cada 15 minutos de preparo somados, no máximo 20 |

Se dois pedidos tiverem a mesma nota, há regras de desempate: primeiro o que tem horário prometido mais cedo, depois o que chegou primeiro.

## Os status do pedido

```
recebido → preparando → pronto → retirado
    ↓
cancelado (só dá pra cancelar enquanto está "recebido")
```

Não dá para pular etapa nem repetir etapa. Quem barra isso é o **servidor**, não só a tela.

## A parte técnica exigida (seção 9 do teste)

O projeto tem duas partes:

**1. API (o "servidor", o cérebro)**
- **Node.js 22 + JavaScript**: a linguagem.
- **Express**: biblioteca que recebe os pedidos da tela, como "me dá a fila" ou "muda o status do pedido 5".
- **PostgreSQL 16**: o banco de dados onde os pedidos ficam guardados.
- **Sequelize 6**: ferramenta para o JavaScript conversar com o banco. Os **migrations** são scripts que criam as tabelas passo a passo.
- **Jest**: ferramenta de testes automáticos.

**2. Web (a tela que o expeditor vê)**
- **React 19 + TypeScript**: para construir a tela.
- **Vite**: ferramenta que roda o React durante o desenvolvimento.
- **MUI 7**: biblioteca de componentes visuais prontos (tabelas, botões), com cara de painel de operação.

**Docker** sobe o banco de dados com um único comando.

## A exigência mais importante

O teste pede para organizar o servidor em **camadas**, cada uma com uma função:
- **Endpoint**: só recebe o pedido e devolve a resposta.
- **Module**: onde ficam as regras (cálculo da nota, regras de status).
- **Repository**: só busca e salva no banco.
- **Schema**: a definição das tabelas.

Eles vão avaliar se as regras estão no lugar certo. Na entrevista, vão pedir uma **mudança ao vivo**, por exemplo "agora VIP vale 30 pontos". Se o projeto estiver bem organizado, isso vira a troca de uma linha.

## O que entregar

- O código, com testes.
- **README.md**: como rodar o projeto.
- **DECISIONS.md**: as decisões que você tomou e por quê, incluindo uma sugestão da IA que você aceitou e uma que rejeitou.
- **ai-logs/**: as conversas com a IA. Esta conversa vai para lá.

**Prazo sugerido:** 4 horas. Eles preferem algo menor que você saiba explicar a algo grande que você não saiba.

Faz sentido até aqui? Se quiser, explico melhor alguma parte, como as camadas ou o cálculo da nota com um exemplo. Quando estiver claro, sigo para a pesquisa de referências e o plano.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about Express 5's async error handling for rejected promises:

## Key Features

Express 5 introduces a significant improvement for developers using async/await by automatically forwarding rejected promises to error-handling middleware. This change eliminates the need for repetitive try/catch blocks, making code cleaner and reducing boilerplate.

## How It Works

In Express 4, developers had to manually handle promise rejections with try/catch blocks and call `next(err)`. In Express 5, if a promise fails, the error is automatically forwarded to your global error-handling middleware, eliminating the need for explicit try-catch blocks.

If fetchData throws an error or rejects, Express will automatically pass the error to the error-handling middleware. This eliminates the need to call next with the error manually.

## Important Limitations

Express 5 added support for returned rejected promises from errors raised in middleware. This does not include calling next from returned resolved promises. Additionally, best practice is to handle errors as close to the site as possible. So while this is now handled in the router, it's best to catch the error in the middleware and handle it without relying on separate error-handling middleware.

I found relevant information about the Node.js best practices by Yoni Goldberg. Here are the key concepts:

## Structure by Components

The root of a system should contain folders or repositories that represent reasonably sized business modules, with each component representing a product domain (bounded context), like 'user-component', 'order-component', etc. Each component has its own API, logic, and logical database.

The approach involves creating basic borders between components, assigning a folder or repository in your system root for each business component and making it self-contained, with other components allowed to consume its functionality only through its public interface or API.

## Layering Components (3-Tier Architecture)

Each component should contain 'layers' - a dedicated object for the web, logic, and data access code. This not only draws a clean separation of concerns but also significantly eases mocking and testing the system.

A common pitfall is that API developers tend to mix layers by passing the web layer objects (e.g. Express req, res) to business logic and data layers - this makes your application dependent on and accessible only by specific web frameworks.

These practices from the Node.js best practices repository help maintain modularity, reduce dependencies between components, and make the codebase easier to manage and scale.

# Recommended Folder Structure and Layering

## Structure by Components (Good Approach)

The document recommends organizing your application into self-contained components rather than by technical role. Here's the recommended structure:

```
my-system
├─ apps (components)
│  ├─ orders
│  │ ├─ package.json
│  │ ├─ api
│  │ ├─ domain
│  │ ├─ data-access
│  ├─ users
│  ├─ payments
├─ libraries (generic cross-component functionality)
│  ├─ logger
│  ├─ authenticator
```

## Key Layering Principles

Each component should include:
- **API layer** - public interface for other components
- **Domain layer** - business logic
- **Data-access layer** - database interactions

## What to Avoid (Bad Approach)

Don't organize by technical role:
```
my-system
├─ controllers
├─ services
├─ models
```

## Core Rationale

"Monolithic applications can be successively deployed, but increasingly people feel frustrations with them—especially as more applications are deployed to the cloud. Change cycles are tied together; scaling requires scaling of the entire application rather than parts of it that require greater resource."

This component-based structure keeps code modular, makes onboarding easier, and establishes foundations for potential microservices migration as applications grow.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about Sequelize 6 and conditional updates with optimistic concurrency:

## Sequelize 6 Optimistic Locking

Sequelize has built-in support for optimistic locking through a model instance version count. Optimistic locking is disabled by default and can be enabled by setting the version property to true in a specific model definition or global model configuration.

## How It Works

Optimistic locking allows concurrent access to model records for edits and prevents conflicts from overwriting data by checking whether another process has made changes to a record since it was read and throws an OptimisticLockError when a conflict is detected.

## Implementation with Conditional Updates

When using `Model.update()` with a WHERE clause for conditional updates, you can implement optimistic locking by:

1. **Including a version check in the WHERE clause** - Include the expected version number in your WHERE condition
2. **Incrementing the version on update** - Include `version: version + 1` in the update values
3. **Checking affectedCount** - Verify the number of affected rows to determine if the update succeeded (a return of 0 rows indicates a conflict)

The affectedCount returned from `Model.update()` can be checked to determine if the update was successful, since an optimistic lock conflict would result in zero rows being updated.

The official Sequelize v6 documentation on optimistic locking can be found at: https://sequelize.org/docs/v6/other-topics/optimistic-locking/

## Key Findings:

**Configuration with .sequelizerc:**
You can define CLI flags in a .sequelizerc file, which can be either a JSON file or a Node.JS script that exports a hash. An example configuration might define the config path and migrations-path.

**Sequelize CLI Commands:**
sequelize-cli can be installed globally or locally to your node_modules folder. The db:seed command runs seeders.

**PostgreSQL Timezone Handling:**
When storing Sequelize.DATE data into the DB, the concern is that data may be stored in local time or the machine's timezone rather than UTC. Sequelize has poor-to-no-support for the timestamp without timezone column type in Postgres.

**Potential Solutions:**
Two suggested solutions are: 1) disable date parsing by the application entirely and pull all such fields as strings, or 2) force UTC conversion when pulling the fields from the database.

The search results suggest that handling TIMESTAMPTZ vs DATE with UTC in Sequelize migrations requires careful configuration, particularly around how PostgreSQL handles timezone conversions.

Based on the search results, I found information about both approaches to testing time-dependent code:

## Jest's `useFakeTimers` Approach

Jest's `useFakeTimers()` instructs Jest to use fake versions of the global date, performance, time and timer APIs. Fake timers will swap out Date, performance.now(), queueMicrotask(), setImmediate(), clearImmediate(), setInterval(), clearInterval(), setTimeout(), and clearTimeout() with an implementation that gets its time from the fake clock.

You can use jest.useFakeTimers(fakeTimersConfig?) to mock timers in tests. The configuration accepts a `now` parameter (number or Date) that specifies the system time the fake timers will use, defaulting to Date.now().

However, this is a global operation and will affect other tests within the same file.

## Injecting Clock/Now Parameter Approach

An alternative strategy involves passing time through the production code explicitly. The clock injection approach involves passing the time through the production code's clock or now parameter where one exists. Where production code reads the clock directly, a real clock dependency should be added, not a test-only branch.

## Comparison

The injected parameter approach makes your functions **pure** (they depend on passed-in values rather than global state), while `jest.useFakeTimers()` provides a more automatic approach at the cost of making functions dependent on global mocked objects. The search results suggest both have merits depending on your testing strategy and code architecture.

## Key Implementation Patterns

A common approach uses a transition table object where events map to current states and their corresponding next states. For example, with order states like Pending, Processing, Shipped, and Delivered, you can define transitions with `const transitions` that map events to state changes.

## Basic Structure

The simplest implementation checks the current state and event with conditional logic to determine the next state. However, a more organized approach uses nested objects where `transitions[event][currentState]` returns the next state, allowing you to check `if (nextState)` to validate the transition.

## Real-World Order Example

A typical order state machine includes states like New, Paid, Shipped, Delivered, and Cancelled, with transitions for events like Pay, Ship, Deliver, PaymentDeclined, and Cancel. For cancel operations, the state can only be cancelled if the order was in certain states like Pending or Processing.

## Benefits

FSMs provide clarity and organization by breaking down complex behavior into states and transitions, making the codebase more comprehensible and easier to follow. The finite state machine pattern works regardless of whether you use React, Vue, or Angular, and can be implemented without much trouble.

Based on the search results, here's comprehensive information about RFC 9457:

## Overview

RFC 9457 defines a "problem detail" to carry machine-readable details of errors in HTTP response content to avoid the need to define new error response formats for HTTP APIs. This document obsoletes RFC 7807.

## Key Purpose

HTTP status codes cannot always convey enough information about errors to be helpful. Clients need both the machine-readable status code that drives control flow, and structured error detail that drives the response. RFC 9457 is the bridge − standardising the detail layer on top of the status code layer.

## Standard Fields

RFC 9457 defines fields including: type (URI identifying the problem type; required), title (short human-readable summary; recommended), status (the HTTP status code; recommended), detail (human-readable explanation specific to this occurrence; optional), and instance (URI identifying this specific occurrence for log correlation; optional).

## Machine-Readable Format

RFC 9457, previously RFC-7807, is a new standard that defines a common format for error responses in RESTful APIs. It provides a standard way to represent error responses in a consistent and machine-readable format. When returning a Problem Details object, the server should use the Content-Type application/problem+json.

## Framework Support

The Spring Framework supports the "Problem Details for HTTP APIs" specification, RFC 9457. Additionally, Spring Boot 3.x supports it natively through the ProblemDetail class.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about when to use MUI Table vs DataGrid:

## Table vs DataGrid

The DataGrid component is designed for use-cases that are focused on handling large amounts of tabular data. While it comes with a more rigid structure, in exchange, you gain more powerful features.

In contrast, the Table component has a close mapping to the native HTML elements. This constraint makes building rich data tables challenging.

### Decision Guide:

- Use Grid to control layout and positioning
- Use DataGrid when you're displaying structured data like tables

### Table Size and Density

For the Table component specifically, you can control its visual density with the `size` prop (options include "small", "medium", "large") and customize spacing, while dense layouts help display more data per screen space.

### Sticky Header

A sticky header becomes mandatory the moment a table is tall enough that the column titles scroll out of view. Without it, users scroll back up just to remember which column they are reading. Both the Table component (via the `stickyHeader` prop) and DataGrid support sticky headers.

### For Dashboards

When considering data density per screen, tables support high data density, making the Table component with `size="small"` and `stickyHeader` a good choice for dashboard scenarios where you want to display more information compactly while keeping headers visible during scrolling. Use DataGrid when you need advanced features like sorting, filtering, pagination, and handling larger datasets.

I found several helpful resources about Jest, Supertest, Express, and Sequelize integration testing with real PostgreSQL databases:

## Key Testing Patterns

A `pretest` npm script is automatically invoked when the `npm test` command is invoked, and can be used to change the environment to test and refresh the database before each test runs.

The `migrate:reset` command is responsible for refreshing the database before each test runs. Here's an example npm script configuration:

```json
"scripts": {
  "test": "cross-env NODE_ENV=test jest --testTimeout=10000",
  "pretest": "cross-env NODE_ENV=test npm run migrate:reset",
  "migrate:reset": "npx sequelize-cli db:migrate:undo:all && npm run migrate"
}
```

Cross-env is used as an operating system agnostic package for setting environment variables, specifically to set NODE_ENV to test so the test can use the test database.

## Performance Optimization Alternative

A recommended approach for faster tests is to use Sequelize Transactions, where you create a transaction before each test and pass that transaction to each query you run in the test. This avoids the slower approach of running `await sequelize.sync({ force: true })` after each test, which is slow because it drops all tables and recreates them.

## Real Examples

Several GitHub repositories demonstrate complete implementations:
- Eden is an example of a very basic REST API with integration tests.
- There are ExpressJS and Sequelize applications tested with supertest, migrations and seeds.

Several GitHub repositories demonstrate complete implementations:
- Eden is an example of a very basic REST API with integration tests.
- There are ExpressJS and Sequelize applications tested with supertest, migrations and seeds.

References gathered before planning. Each item: what we take from it.

## Environment check (local machine)

| Tool | Local / latest on npm | Spec requires | Action |
|---|---|---|---|
| Node | v24.13.0 local | **Node 22** | Install Node 22 (nvm-windows / fnm), add `.nvmrc` + `engines` |
| @mui/material | 9.4.0 latest | **MUI 7** | Pin `@mui/material@^7` (+ matching `@mui/icons-material@^7`) |
| express | 5.2.1 | Express (no version) | Use Express 5: rejected promises reach the error middleware natively |
| sequelize / sequelize-cli | 6.37.8 / 6.6.5 | Sequelize 6 | OK |
| react / vite | 19.3.0 / 8.3.3 | React 19 / Vite | OK (check Vite 8 vs Vitest compatibility if doing the extra) |
| jest / supertest | 30.5.2 / 7.3.1 | Jest | OK |
| Docker / git | 29.7 / 2.52 | Docker | OK |

## Architecture

- **goldbergyoni/nodebestpractices — "Structure by components" + "Layer your components"**
  https://github.com/goldbergyoni/nodebestpractices/blob/master/sections/projectstructre/breakintcomponents.md
  Group by business component (`orders/`), each with web / domain / data-access layers. Never pass `req`/`res` into the domain layer.
  → We use the spec's names (endpoint / module / repository / schema) inside an `orders` component.
- Layered Express + Sequelize examples (route → controller → service → repository):
  https://github.com/Faeshal/nodejs-layered-architecture ·
  https://github.com/sujeet-agrahari/node-express-modular-architecture
  → Confirms the pattern; we keep it lighter (no DI container, no base classes).

## Express 5 errors

- https://expressjs.com/en/blog/2024-10-15-v5-release/ — async handlers that throw/reject go to the error middleware, no try/catch wrappers.
  → One `AppError(code, httpStatus, message)` class + one error middleware that maps it to `{ error: { code, message } }`.
- RFC 9457 Problem Details: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457 — standard error shape.
  → Considered; spec only asks for a stable `code`. We keep a simple `{ error: { code, message, details? } }` and mention RFC 9457 as a "Next" item. (Decision to record.)

## Business rules

- State machine as a plain transition table (no XState):
  https://techhub.iodigital.com/articles/finite-state-machines-in-javascript
  → `const TRANSITIONS = { start: { from: 'received', to: 'preparing' }, ... }` — one-line change for the live panel.
- Injected clock vs fake timers:
  https://jestjs.io/docs/jest-object (useFakeTimers is global state) ·
  https://github.com/vouchington/vouchington/issues/2151 ("time logic uses an injected clock")
  → `computeScore(order, now)`; endpoint passes `new Date()`; tests pass a fixed Date. No fake timers needed.

## Data / Sequelize

- Concurrency on transitions: https://sequelize.org/docs/v6/other-topics/optimistic-locking/
  → Conditional update `UPDATE orders SET status=:to WHERE id=:id AND status=:from`; `affectedCount === 0` ⇒ re-read and report `INVALID_TRANSITION`. Simpler than a version column.
- Dates: Postgres `timestamp with time zone`; Sequelize `DATE` maps to `TIMESTAMPTZ` on postgres. https://mattbatman.com/sequelize-postgres-and-dates/
- `.sequelizerc` to point CLI to `src/schema/{migrations,seeders,models}`.

## Tests

- Integration tests with real Postgres + supertest + migrations:
  https://github.com/peretch/testing-express-sequelize ·
  https://jaygould.co.uk/2020-07-28-jest-sequelize-testing-dedicated-database/
  → Priority tests: pure, no DB. Transition rules: pure unit tests on the module. Plus a small supertest suite against a separate test DB (`kitchen_queue_test` on the same container) for HTTP codes + queue exclusion. Close the Sequelize connection in `afterAll` (known Jest hang).

## Monorepo / DX

- npm workspaces + `concurrently`: https://github.com/AlessandroAlbi/vite-react-express-api-monorepo-bp ·
  https://earthly.dev/blog/npm-workspaces-monorepo/
  → Root `package.json` with `workspaces: ["api","web"]`; `npm install` once; `npm run db:setup`; `npm run dev` = concurrently api + web. Vite proxy `/orders` → `:4000` (avoids CORS config).

## UI

- MUI Table docs: https://mui.com/material-ui/react-table/
  → Plain `Table size="small" stickyHeader` (DataGrid would re-sort client-side and is overkill; spec forbids reordering).

## Extras (if time)

- Playwright webServer array (starts sequentially): https://playwright.dev/docs/test-webserver

# CLAUDE.md — Kitchen Display Queue (take-home test)

Full assignment, verbatim: `docs/SPEC.md`. **When in doubt, re-read the spec — it wins over this file.**

## What is being graded (read before every decision)

1. **Organization:** business rules live in the right layer.
2. **Explainability:** the author must explain *every* file and function in a live panel. Prefer simple, obvious code over clever code. No unnecessary dependencies, abstractions or files.
3. **Changeability:** in the panel they will make a **live product change to ranking or status rules**. Changing a weight, bucket, cap, tie-break or transition must be a **one-place edit** (config table / transition map), covered by tests.
4. **Honesty:** 4-hour time box. Smaller + honest `DECISIONS.md` beats wide + unexplainable. Do NOT expand scope.

## Fixed tech stack (do not substitute)

- **API:** Node.js 22, **JavaScript** (not TS), Express, Sequelize 6 **with migrations (never `sync()`)**, PostgreSQL 16, Jest.
- **Web:** Vite, React 19, TypeScript, **MUI 7**, Vitest (extra only).
- **DB:** `docker-compose.yml` with **only** Postgres 16, host port **5433**, user/pass/db = `kitchen_queue` (exact YAML in spec §9.3).
- Ports: API **4000**, web **5173**.
- One repo, two apps. No private/external repo dependencies.

## API layers (mandatory)

| Layer | Responsibility | Must NOT |
|---|---|---|
| Endpoint | HTTP only: read req, call module, write res. Thin. | contain rules |
| Module | Priority scoring, state machine, queue sorting | touch Sequelize |
| Repository | Sequelize queries, includes, filters | contain rules |
| Schema | Sequelize models + migrations | |

- Priority function is **pure**: `(orderData, now) => number`. Tests run **without Postgres and without mocking Sequelize**.

## Data model

- **MenuItem:** `name` unique non-empty; `category` ∈ starter|main_course|dessert|drink; `prep_time_minutes` int > 0. Seed only, no CRUD.
- **Order:** `customer_name` non-empty; `type` ∈ dine_in|takeout|delivery; `placed_at` set on creation; `promised_at` nullable (relevant for delivery/takeout); `is_vip` bool; `status` ∈ received|preparing|ready|picked_up|cancelled.
- **OrderItem:** `order_id` FK, `menu_item_id` FK, `quantity` int > 0.
- Enforce constraints in the DB too (CHECK / NOT NULL / UNIQUE / FK). Timestamps as `TIMESTAMPTZ`, UTC everywhere.

## Priority score (spec §5)

score = type + vip + wait + promised + complexity

- type: dine_in 30, takeout 20, delivery 10
- vip: +20
- wait: `min(40, floor(minutes_waiting/10)*5)`; `minutes_waiting` = **whole minutes floored** (9m50s → 9 → 0 pts)
- promised: ≤30 min from now → 25; 31–60 → 15; >60 or null → 0
- complexity: `min(20, floor(total_prep/15)*5)`, `total_prep = Σ prep_time_minutes * quantity`
- Tie-break: earlier `promised_at` (null last) → earlier `placed_at` → smaller `id`.
- Computed **at request time**: real clock in app, **frozen `now` injected** in tests. Never `Date.now()` inside the pure function.
- Worked examples A and B (spec §5.3) both = 60, B ranks above A → must be literal test cases.

## State machine (spec §6)

received→preparing, received→cancelled, preparing→ready, ready→picked_up. **Everything else rejected**, including:
skipping steps, repeating same status (start on preparing = error, not silent success), any move from terminal (picked_up, cancelled).
Enforced **on the server** (module), not only by hiding buttons.

## API (spec §7)

| Method | Path | Behavior |
|---|---|---|
| GET | `/orders/queue` | default received+preparing sorted by score; `?status=received\|preparing`; each order includes `score` |
| POST | `/orders/:id/start` | received → preparing |
| POST | `/orders/:id/ready` | preparing → ready |
| POST | `/orders/:id/pickup` | ready → picked_up |
| POST | `/orders/:id/cancel` | received → cancelled |

Errors: 4xx + **stable machine-readable code** (e.g. `INVALID_TRANSITION`, `ORDER_NOT_FOUND`, invalid status filter, invalid id). **Document codes in README.**

## UI (spec §8) — one page, Kitchen Display, MUI, dense ops-dashboard look

- [ ] Table: score, customer name, order type, items summary, wait time, promised time, VIP badge, status
- [ ] Filter: active (default) / received / preparing
- [ ] Only the valid next action per row
- [ ] Cancel for `received` orders
- [ ] Empty state
- [ ] API errors visible on screen (not console)
- [ ] **No scoring formula in the UI**; render rows in exactly the API order

## Seed (spec §9.5)

Dates **relative to UTC now at seed time** (no hard-coded dates). Must demonstrate:
- [ ] all 3 types · [ ] VIP + non-VIP · [ ] wait-time cap (≥80 min waiting) · [ ] complexity cap (≥60 prep min)
- [ ] score tie broken by `promised_at` (keep the tie stable as time passes — same `placed_at` / same bucket behaviour)
- [ ] statuses received, preparing, and ≥1 `ready` (not in active queue)

## Required tests (spec §10)

- **Jest priority:** score calc, wait cap, complexity cap, all 4 promised buckets (≤30, 31–60, >60, null), tie-break, lower-base-type-wins case (delivery VIP tight promise beats dine_in non-VIP). **Frozen `now`.**
- **Jest transitions:** every legal transition succeeds; illegal rejected (skip, repeat, from terminal); cancelled/picked_up not in default queue.

## Developer experience (spec §9.4) — README must allow, from a clean machine:

1. `docker compose up -d` 2. one install command 3. one `db:setup` (migrate + seed) 4. one dev command (API + web together)

## Deliverables checklist (spec §12)

- [ ] `README.md`: prerequisites (Docker, Node 22), the 4 commands, ports, API error codes
- [ ] `DECISIONS.md` with sections: **Scope, Layers, Priority, Transitions, AI, Next** (short paragraphs each)
  - Layers: name one rule refused in the UI and why
  - Priority: how score is produced at request time + one easy-to-get-wrong edge case
  - Transitions: where enforced + what happens on start of an already-preparing order
  - AI: one suggestion kept + one rejected/rewritten, **quote the idea**
  - Next: two changes for a real kitchen (not implemented)
  - Note extras attempted/skipped; justify any deviation from suggested layout
- [ ] `ai-logs/` at root with **full** AI conversation exports (Claude Code session `.jsonl` / markdown)
- [ ] API, web, migrations, seed, tests

## Extras (only after core is solid)

1. `POST /orders` (validate items non-empty, menu_item_id exists, quantity positive int, ≥1 Jest validation test)
2. Vitest component test (cancel only for received, or empty state)
3. Playwright happy path with `webServer`, `npm run test:e2e`

## Out of scope — do NOT build

Auth/users/roles, payments, customer entity, pagination, design-system package, Storybook, CI, Restify, Redis, background jobs, WebSockets/real-time, pixel-perfect visuals.

## Open ambiguities (decide explicitly, record in DECISIONS.md)

- `promised_at` already in the past (overdue): 25 pts? (likely yes: "within 30 minutes" includes overdue — most urgent)
- Bucket boundaries: exactly 30 min → 25; 30m01s–60m → 15? Compare in ms or whole minutes?
- `promised_at` on `dine_in`: count it or ignore it?
- `placed_at` in the future (clock skew): clamp wait to 0.
- Concurrent transitions (two clicks on start): conditional UPDATE `WHERE status = from` / row lock.
- Invalid `?status=` value (e.g. `ready`) → 400 with code.

## Working rules for Claude

- Communicate with the user in Portuguese; code, comments, docs in English.
- Keep this checklist updated as items are completed.
- Every AI suggestion kept/rejected that is notable → note it for DECISIONS.md "AI" section.

A pesquisa está pronta e o resumo está salvo em `docs/RESEARCH.md`, com os links. Abaixo, em linguagem simples.

## ⚠️ Dois problemas no seu computador

1. **Versão do Node.** O teste exige **Node 22** e o seu computador tem o **Node 24**. Precisamos instalar o 22 lado a lado (com uma ferramenta como o `nvm-windows` ou o `fnm`) e marcar no projeto que ele usa o 22. Se o avaliador rodar no 22 e algo quebrar, isso conta contra você.
2. **Versão do MUI.** A versão mais nova do MUI já é a 9, mas o teste pede a **7**. Se instalarmos sem dizer a versão, vem a 9. Vou fixar a 7.

## O que aprendi nas referências e como vamos usar

**1. Organização do servidor** ([Node.js Best Practices](https://github.com/goldbergyoni/nodebestpractices/blob/master/sections/projectstructre/breakintcomponents.md), um guia muito usado na comunidade)
- O guia recomenda agrupar o código por assunto ("pedidos") e, dentro dele, separar em camadas. É o mesmo que o teste pede.
- O erro mais comum é passar os objetos de requisição do Express para dentro das regras de negócio. As regras devem ser funções que não sabem que existe internet.
- Exemplos reais que seguem o padrão: [nodejs-layered-architecture](https://github.com/Faeshal/nodejs-layered-architecture) e [node-express-modular-architecture](https://github.com/sujeet-agrahari/node-express-modular-architecture).

**2. Express 5** ([anúncio oficial](https://expressjs.com/en/blog/2024-10-15-v5-release/))
- Na versão 5, quando algo dá errado, o erro vai sozinho para um tratador central de erros. Isso evita repetir `try/catch` em toda rota e deixa as rotas bem finas, como o teste pede.

**3. Regras de status** ([artigo sobre máquinas de estado](https://techhub.iodigital.com/articles/finite-state-machines-in-javascript))
- Existem bibliotecas para isso (como o XState), mas seriam exagero aqui. Uma **tabela simples** basta: "start: de recebido para preparando". Se na entrevista pedirem "agora dá pra cancelar pedido em preparo", é uma linha.

**4. Testar o "agora"** ([documentação do Jest](https://jestjs.io/docs/jest-object))
- Uma opção é "fingir o relógio" no teste. A outra, mais limpa, é **passar o "agora" como parâmetro** para a função de nota. O teste exige essa segunda forma: a função tem que ser "pura".

**5. Dois cliques ao mesmo tempo** ([Sequelize](https://sequelize.org/docs/v6/other-topics/optimistic-locking/))
- Se duas pessoas clicam em "começar" juntas, as duas não podem conseguir. A solução simples é o banco só aceitar a mudança se o pedido ainda estiver no status esperado. Se não mudou nenhuma linha, devolvemos erro. Não é pedido no teste, mas mostra cuidado e é fácil de explicar.

**6. Testes com banco** ([exemplo](https://github.com/peretch/testing-express-sequelize))
- Os testes da nota e da tabela de status rodam sem banco nenhum.
- Também faremos alguns testes que chamam a API de verdade, com um banco de testes separado, para provar que um pedido cancelado não aparece na fila.

**7. Um comando para tudo** ([exemplo de monorepo](https://github.com/AlessandroAlbi/vite-react-express-api-monorepo-bp))
- O **npm workspaces** permite um único `npm install` na raiz instalar API e tela. A ferramenta **concurrently** roda os dois juntos com `npm run dev`. Isso cobre os 4 comandos que o teste exige.

**8. Tabela da tela** ([MUI Table](https://mui.com/material-ui/react-table/))
- O MUI tem uma tabela simples e uma avançada (DataGrid). Vamos usar a **simples, no modo compacto**. A avançada reordena as linhas sozinha, e o teste proíbe a tela de mudar a ordem que vem da API.

**9. Formato dos erros** ([RFC 9457](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457))
- Existe um padrão oficial para respostas de erro. Vamos usar um formato mais simples, `{ error: { code, message } }`, porque o teste só pede um código estável. O padrão oficial pode aparecer como sugestão na seção "Next" do `DECISIONS.md`.

**Próximo passo:** montar o plano em etapas. Antes, uma pergunta: **você quer que eu instale o Node 22 agora** ou prefere fazer isso você mesma? Posso te guiar passo a passo.

# CLAUDE.md — Kitchen Display Queue (take-home test)

Full assignment, verbatim: `docs/SPEC.md`. **When in doubt, re-read the spec — it wins over this file.**

## What is being graded (read before every decision)

1. **Organization:** business rules live in the right layer.
2. **Explainability:** the author must explain *every* file and function in a live panel. Prefer simple, obvious code over clever code. No unnecessary dependencies, abstractions or files.
3. **Changeability:** in the panel they will make a **live product change to ranking or status rules**. Changing a weight, bucket, cap, tie-break or transition must be a **one-place edit** (config table / transition map), covered by tests.
4. **Honesty:** 4-hour time box. Smaller + honest `DECISIONS.md` beats wide + unexplainable. Do NOT expand scope.

## Fixed tech stack (do not substitute)

- **API:** Node.js 22, **JavaScript** (not TS), Express, Sequelize 6 **with migrations (never `sync()`)**, PostgreSQL 16, Jest.
- **Web:** Vite, React 19, TypeScript, **MUI 7**, Vitest (extra only).
- **DB:** `docker-compose.yml` with **only** Postgres 16, host port **5433**, user/pass/db = `kitchen_queue` (exact YAML in spec §9.3).
- Ports: API **4000**, web **5173**.
- ⚠️ Local machine has Node 24 → must use Node 22 (`.nvmrc` + `engines`). npm latest MUI is 9 → **pin `@mui/material@^7`**. See `docs/RESEARCH.md`.
- One repo, two apps. No private/external repo dependencies.

## API layers (mandatory)

| Layer | Responsibility | Must NOT |
|---|---|---|
| Endpoint | HTTP only: read req, call module, write res. Thin. | contain rules |
| Module | Priority scoring, state machine, queue sorting | touch Sequelize |
| Repository | Sequelize queries, includes, filters | contain rules |
| Schema | Sequelize models + migrations | |

- Priority function is **pure**: `(orderData, now) => number`. Tests run **without Postgres and without mocking Sequelize**.

## Data model

- **MenuItem:** `name` unique non-empty; `category` ∈ starter|main_course|dessert|drink; `prep_time_minutes` int > 0. Seed only, no CRUD.
- **Order:** `customer_name` non-empty; `type` ∈ dine_in|takeout|delivery; `placed_at` set on creation; `promised_at` nullable (relevant for delivery/takeout); `is_vip` bool; `status` ∈ received|preparing|ready|picked_up|cancelled.
- **OrderItem:** `order_id` FK, `menu_item_id` FK, `quantity` int > 0.
- Enforce constraints in the DB too (CHECK / NOT NULL / UNIQUE / FK). Timestamps as `TIMESTAMPTZ`, UTC everywhere.

## Priority score (spec §5)

score = type + vip + wait + promised + complexity

- type: dine_in 30, takeout 20, delivery 10
- vip: +20
- wait: `min(40, floor(minutes_waiting/10)*5)`; `minutes_waiting` = **whole minutes floored** (9m50s → 9 → 0 pts)
- promised: ≤30 min from now → 25; 31–60 → 15; >60 or null → 0
- complexity: `min(20, floor(total_prep/15)*5)`, `total_prep = Σ prep_time_minutes * quantity`
- Tie-break: earlier `promised_at` (null last) → earlier `placed_at` → smaller `id`.
- Computed **at request time**: real clock in app, **frozen `now` injected** in tests. Never `Date.now()` inside the pure function.
- Worked examples A and B (spec §5.3) both = 60, B ranks above A → must be literal test cases.

## State machine (spec §6)

received→preparing, received→cancelled, preparing→ready, ready→picked_up. **Everything else rejected**, including:
skipping steps, repeating same status (start on preparing = error, not silent success), any move from terminal (picked_up, cancelled).
Enforced **on the server** (module), not only by hiding buttons.

## API (spec §7)

| Method | Path | Behavior |
|---|---|---|
| GET | `/orders/queue` | default received+preparing sorted by score; `?status=received\|preparing`; each order includes `score` |
| POST | `/orders/:id/start` | received → preparing |
| POST | `/orders/:id/ready` | preparing → ready |
| POST | `/orders/:id/pickup` | ready → picked_up |
| POST | `/orders/:id/cancel` | received → cancelled |

Errors: 4xx + **stable machine-readable code** (e.g. `INVALID_TRANSITION`, `ORDER_NOT_FOUND`, invalid status filter, invalid id). **Document codes in README.**

## UI (spec §8) — one page, Kitchen Display, MUI, dense ops-dashboard look

- [ ] Table: score, customer name, order type, items summary, wait time, promised time, VIP badge, status
- [ ] Filter: active (default) / received / preparing
- [ ] Only the valid next action per row
- [ ] Cancel for `received` orders
- [ ] Empty state
- [ ] API errors visible on screen (not console)
- [ ] **No scoring formula in the UI**; render rows in exactly the API order

## Seed (spec §9.5)

Dates **relative to UTC now at seed time** (no hard-coded dates). Must demonstrate:
- [ ] all 3 types · [ ] VIP + non-VIP · [ ] wait-time cap (≥80 min waiting) · [ ] complexity cap (≥60 prep min)
- [ ] score tie broken by `promised_at` (keep the tie stable as time passes — same `placed_at` / same bucket behaviour)
- [ ] statuses received, preparing, and ≥1 `ready` (not in active queue)

## Required tests (spec §10)

- **Jest priority:** score calc, wait cap, complexity cap, all 4 promised buckets (≤30, 31–60, >60, null), tie-break, lower-base-type-wins case (delivery VIP tight promise beats dine_in non-VIP). **Frozen `now`.**
- **Jest transitions:** every legal transition succeeds; illegal rejected (skip, repeat, from terminal); cancelled/picked_up not in default queue.

## Developer experience (spec §9.4) — README must allow, from a clean machine:

1. `docker compose up -d` 2. one install command 3. one `db:setup` (migrate + seed) 4. one dev command (API + web together)

## Deliverables checklist (spec §12)

- [ ] `README.md`: prerequisites (Docker, Node 22), the 4 commands, ports, API error codes
- [ ] `DECISIONS.md` with sections: **Scope, Layers, Priority, Transitions, AI, Next** (short paragraphs each)
  - Layers: name one rule refused in the UI and why
  - Priority: how score is produced at request time + one easy-to-get-wrong edge case
  - Transitions: where enforced + what happens on start of an already-preparing order
  - AI: one suggestion kept + one rejected/rewritten, **quote the idea**
  - Next: two changes for a real kitchen (not implemented)
  - Note extras attempted/skipped; justify any deviation from suggested layout
- [ ] `ai-logs/` at root with **full** AI conversation exports (Claude Code session `.jsonl` / markdown)
- [ ] API, web, migrations, seed, tests

## Extras (only after core is solid)

1. `POST /orders` (validate items non-empty, menu_item_id exists, quantity positive int, ≥1 Jest validation test)
2. Vitest component test (cancel only for received, or empty state)
3. Playwright happy path with `webServer`, `npm run test:e2e`

## Out of scope — do NOT build

Auth/users/roles, payments, customer entity, pagination, design-system package, Storybook, CI, Restify, Redis, background jobs, WebSockets/real-time, pixel-perfect visuals.

## Open ambiguities (decide explicitly, record in DECISIONS.md)

- `promised_at` already in the past (overdue): 25 pts? (likely yes: "within 30 minutes" includes overdue — most urgent)
- Bucket boundaries: exactly 30 min → 25; 30m01s–60m → 15? Compare in ms or whole minutes?
- `promised_at` on `dine_in`: count it or ignore it?
- `placed_at` in the future (clock skew): clamp wait to 0.
- Concurrent transitions (two clicks on start): conditional UPDATE `WHERE status = from` / row lock.
- Invalid `?status=` value (e.g. `ready`) → 400 with code.

## Working rules for Claude

- Communicate with the user in Portuguese; code, comments, docs in English.
- Keep this checklist updated as items are completed.
- Every AI suggestion kept/rejected that is notable → note it for DECISIONS.md "AI" section.

entries.description:
Use this tool proactively when you're about to start a non-trivial implementation task. Getting user sign-off on your approach before writing code prevents wasted effort and ensures alignment. This tool transitions you into plan mode where you can explore the codebase and design an implementation approach for user approval.

## When to Use This Tool

**Prefer using EnterPlanMode** for implementation tasks unless they're simple. Use it when ANY of these conditions apply:

1. **New Feature Implementation**: Adding meaningful new functionality
   - Example: "Add a logout button" - where should it go? What should happen on click?
   - Example: "Add form validation" - what rules? What error messages?

2. **Multiple Valid Approaches**: The task can be solved in several different ways
   - Example: "Add caching to the API" - could use Redis, in-memory, file-based, etc.
   - Example: "Improve performance" - many optimization strategies possible

3. **Code Modifications**: Changes that affect existing behavior or structure
   - Example: "Update the login flow" - what exactly should change?
   - Example: "Refactor this component" - what's the target architecture?

4. **Architectural Decisions**: The task requires choosing between patterns or technologies
   - Example: "Add real-time updates" - WebSockets vs SSE vs polling
   - Example: "Implement state management" - Redux vs Context vs custom solution

5. **Multi-File Changes**: The task will likely touch more than 2-3 files
   - Example: "Refactor the authentication system"
   - Example: "Add a new API endpoint with tests"

6. **Unclear Requirements**: You need to explore before understanding the full scope
   - Example: "Make the app faster" - need to profile and identify bottlenecks
   - Example: "Fix the bug in checkout" - need to investigate root cause

7. **User Preferences Matter**: The implementation could reasonably go multiple ways
   - If you would use AskUserQuestion to clarify the approach, use EnterPlanMode instead
   - Plan mode lets you explore first, then present options with context

## When NOT to Use This Tool

Only skip EnterPlanMode for simple tasks:
- Single-line or few-line fixes (typos, obvious bugs, small tweaks)
- Adding a single function with clear requirements
- Tasks where the user has given very specific, detailed instructions
- Pure research/exploration tasks (use the Agent tool instead)

## What Happens in Plan Mode

In plan mode, you'll:
1. Thoroughly explore the codebase using Glob, Grep, and Read
2. Understand existing patterns and architecture
3. Design an implementation approach
4. Present your plan to the user for approval
5. Use AskUserQuestion if you need to clarify approaches
6. Exit plan mode with ExitPlanMode when ready to implement

## Examples

### GOOD - Use EnterPlanMode:
User: "Add user authentication to the app"
- Requires architectural decisions (session vs JWT, where to store tokens, middleware structure)

User: "Optimize the database queries"
- Multiple approaches possible, need to profile first, significant impact

User: "Implement dark mode"
- Architectural decision on theme system, affects many components

User: "Add a delete button to the user profile"
- Seems simple but involves: where to place it, confirmation dialog, API call, error handling, state updates

User: "Update the error handling in the API"
- Affects multiple files, user should approve the approach

### BAD - Don't use EnterPlanMode:
User: "Fix the typo in the README"
- Straightforward, no planning needed

User: "Add a console.log to debug this function"
- Simple, obvious implementation

User: "What files handle routing?"
- Research task, not implementation planning

## Important Notes

- This tool REQUIRES user approval - they must consent to entering plan mode
- If unsure whether to use it, err on the side of planning - it's better to get alignment upfront than to redo work
- Users appreciate being consulted before significant changes are made to their codebase

entries.name: ExitPlanMode
entries.description:
Use this tool when you are in plan mode and have finished writing your plan to the plan file and are ready for user approval.

## How This Tool Works
- You should have already written your plan to the plan file specified in the plan mode system message
- This tool does NOT take the plan content as a parameter - it will read the plan from the file you wrote
- This tool simply signals that you're done planning and ready for the user to review and approve
- The user will see the contents of your plan file when they review it

## When to Use This Tool
IMPORTANT: Only use this tool when the task requires planning the implementation steps of a task that requires writing code. For research tasks where you're gathering information, searching files, reading files or in general trying to understand the codebase - do NOT use this tool.

## Before Using This Tool
Ensure your plan is complete and unambiguous:
- If you have unresolved questions about requirements or approach, use AskUserQuestion first (in earlier phases)
- Once your plan is finalized, use THIS tool to request approval

**Important:** Do NOT use AskUserQuestion to ask "Is this plan okay?" or "Should I proceed?" - that's exactly what THIS tool does. ExitPlanMode inherently requests user approval of your plan.

## Examples

1. Initial task: "Search for and understand the implementation of vim mode in the codebase" - Do not use the exit plan mode tool because you are not planning the implementation steps of a task.
2. Initial task: "Help me implement yank mode for vim" - Use the exit plan mode tool after you have finished planning the implementation steps of the task.
3. Initial task: "Add a new feature to handle user authentication" - If unsure about auth method (OAuth, JWT, etc.), use AskUserQuestion first, then use exit plan mode tool after clarifying the approach.

questions.question: Pedido com horário prometido que JÁ PASSOU (atrasado): quantos pontos de 'promised' ele ganha?

options.label: 25 pontos (Recommended)
options.description: Trata 'atrasado' como 'dentro de 30 min' — é o caso mais urgente, tem que subir na fila. Leitura natural de 'within 30 minutes'.

options.label: 0 pontos
options.description: Leitura literal: só conta se o horário está no futuro. Risco: pedido atrasado cai na fila, o que é ruim pro negócio.

questions.question: Como medir 'faltam X minutos' para o horário prometido? (a tabela diz 'até 30' e '31–60', e não fala de 30min e 30s)

options.label: Minutos inteiros (Recommended)
options.description: Arredonda pra baixo, igual o enunciado manda fazer no tempo de espera. 30m59s = 30 → 25 pts; 31m00s → 15 pts; 60m59s → 15; 61m → 0. Bate exatamente com '0–30 / 31–60' e fica consistente com a outra regra de tempo.

options.label: Milissegundos exatos
options.description: ≤ 30min00s → 25; até 60min00s → 15; acima → 0. Mais preciso, mas 30m01s já cai pra 15 e não bate com o texto '31–60'.

questions.question: Se um pedido 'dine_in' (comer no local) tiver horário prometido preenchido, ele conta na nota?

options.label: Conta normalmente (Recommended)
options.description: A fórmula da nota não depende do tipo. O enunciado só diz que o campo é 'relevante' pra delivery/takeout. Mantemos a função simples e o seed não cria dine_in com horário.

options.label: Ignorar para dine_in
options.description: Interpretação mais restrita: adiciona uma regra extra na função que precisa ser explicada e testada.

options.label: Proibir no banco
options.description: Validar que dine_in não pode ter promised_at. Mais rígido, mais código.

questions.question: Quais pontos extras você quer que a gente tente DEPOIS que o obrigatório estiver pronto e entendido?

options.label: POST /orders
options.description: Criar pedido via API com validações + teste Jest. Reaproveita bem as camadas; risco baixo.

options.label: Teste Vitest
options.description: Teste de componente: botão cancelar só aparece em 'received' / estado vazio. Pequeno.

options.label: Playwright E2E
options.description: Teste ponta-a-ponta abrindo o navegador. Mais configuração, mais pontos de falha.
