# CLAUDE.md — Kitchen Display Queue (take-home test)

Full assignment, verbatim: `docs/SPEC.md`. **When in doubt, re-read the spec — it wins over this file.**

## What is being graded (read before every decision)

1. **Organization:** business rules live in the right layer.
2. **Explainability:** the author must explain *every* file and function in a live panel. Prefer simple, obvious code over clever code. No unnecessary dependencies, abstractions or files.
3. **Changeability:** in the panel they will make a **live product change to ranking or status rules**. Changing a weight, bucket, cap, tie-break or transition must be a **one-place edit** (config table / transition map), covered by tests.
4. **Honesty:** 4-hour time box. Smaller + honest `DECISIONS.md` beats wide + unexplainable. Do NOT expand scope.

## Fixed tech stack (do not substitute)

- **API:** Node.js 22, **JavaScript** (not TS), Express, Sequelize 6 **with migrations (never `sync()`)**, PostgreSQL 16, Jest.
- **Web:** Vite, React 19, TypeScript, **MUI 7**, Vitest (extra only).
- **DB:** `docker-compose.yml` with **only** Postgres 16, host port **5433**, user/pass/db = `kitchen_queue` (exact YAML in spec §9.3).
- Ports: API **4000**, web **5173**.
- ⚠️ Local machine has Node 24 (system) + Node 22 via **fnm** (default, PowerShell profile runs `fnm env --use-on-cd`). Always run node/npm under Node 22: in tool shells verify with `node -v`; if it shows v24, prefix with `fnm exec --using=22 -- <cmd>`. `.nvmrc` = 22; also set `engines`. npm latest MUI is 9 → **pin `@mui/material@^7`**. See `docs/RESEARCH.md`.
- One repo, two apps. No private/external repo dependencies.

## API layers (mandatory)

| Layer | Responsibility | Must NOT |
|---|---|---|
| Endpoint | HTTP only: read req, call module, write res. Thin. | contain rules |
| Module | Priority scoring, state machine, queue sorting | touch Sequelize |
| Repository | Sequelize queries, includes, filters | contain rules |
| Schema | Sequelize models + migrations | |

- Priority function is **pure**: `(orderData, now) => number`. Tests run **without Postgres and without mocking Sequelize**.

## Data model

- **MenuItem:** `name` unique non-empty; `category` ∈ starter|main_course|dessert|drink; `prep_time_minutes` int > 0. Seed only, no CRUD.
- **Order:** `customer_name` non-empty; `type` ∈ dine_in|takeout|delivery; `placed_at` set on creation; `promised_at` nullable (relevant for delivery/takeout); `is_vip` bool; `status` ∈ received|preparing|ready|picked_up|cancelled.
- **OrderItem:** `order_id` FK, `menu_item_id` FK, `quantity` int > 0.
- Enforce constraints in the DB too (CHECK / NOT NULL / UNIQUE / FK). Timestamps as `TIMESTAMPTZ`, UTC everywhere.

## Priority score (spec §5)

score = type + vip + wait + promised + complexity

- type: dine_in 30, takeout 20, delivery 10
- vip: +20
- wait: `min(40, floor(minutes_waiting/10)*5)`; `minutes_waiting` = **whole minutes floored** (9m50s → 9 → 0 pts)
- promised: ≤30 min from now → 25; 31–60 → 15; >60 or null → 0
- complexity: `min(20, floor(total_prep/15)*5)`, `total_prep = Σ prep_time_minutes * quantity`
- Tie-break: earlier `promised_at` (null last) → earlier `placed_at` → smaller `id`.
- Computed **at request time**: real clock in app, **frozen `now` injected** in tests. Never `Date.now()` inside the pure function.
- Worked examples A and B (spec §5.3) both = 60, B ranks above A → must be literal test cases.

## State machine (spec §6)

received→preparing, received→cancelled, preparing→ready, ready→picked_up. **Everything else rejected**, including:
skipping steps, repeating same status (start on preparing = error, not silent success), any move from terminal (picked_up, cancelled).
Enforced **on the server** (module), not only by hiding buttons.

## API (spec §7)

| Method | Path | Behavior |
|---|---|---|
| GET | `/orders/queue` | default received+preparing sorted by score; `?status=received\|preparing`; each order includes `score` |
| POST | `/orders/:id/start` | received → preparing |
| POST | `/orders/:id/ready` | preparing → ready |
| POST | `/orders/:id/pickup` | ready → picked_up |
| POST | `/orders/:id/cancel` | received → cancelled |

Errors: 4xx + **stable machine-readable code** (e.g. `INVALID_TRANSITION`, `ORDER_NOT_FOUND`, invalid status filter, invalid id). **Document codes in README.**

## UI (spec §8) — one page, Kitchen Display, MUI, dense ops-dashboard look

- [ ] Table: score, customer name, order type, items summary, wait time, promised time, VIP badge, status
- [ ] Filter: active (default) / received / preparing
- [ ] Only the valid next action per row
- [ ] Cancel for `received` orders
- [ ] Empty state
- [ ] API errors visible on screen (not console)
- [ ] **No scoring formula in the UI**; render rows in exactly the API order

## Seed (spec §9.5)

Dates **relative to UTC now at seed time** (no hard-coded dates). Must demonstrate:
- [x] all 3 types · [x] VIP + non-VIP · [x] wait-time cap (≥80 min waiting) · [x] complexity cap (≥60 prep min)
- [x] score tie broken by `promised_at` (stable ~2 h: same `placed_at`, both promises in the 0-point bucket)
- [x] statuses received, preparing, and ≥1 `ready` (not in active queue)

# Implementation plan — Kitchen Display Queue

Source of truth: `docs/SPEC.md`. Summary/checklist: `CLAUDE.md`. References: `docs/RESEARCH.md`.

## Context

Take-home test: an API (Node 22 + Express + Sequelize 6 + Postgres 16 + Jest) and a web page
(Vite + React 19 + TS + MUI 7) for a kitchen order queue ranked by a priority score, with status
transitions enforced on the server. Graded on: business rules in the right layer, every file
explainable, and a live change to ranking/status being **local and quick**. Time box: 4 h.

**Golden rule:** every ambiguity is resolved by the most literal reading of the spec. Decisions so far
(they go into DECISIONS.md):
- Overdue `promised_at` → 25 points (the 0-point bucket is defined only as "more than 60 minutes away or null").
- Minutes until the promise = **whole floored minutes**, same rule as `minutes_waiting` → 0–30 = 25, 31–60 = 15, >60 = 0.
- `promised_at` on a `dine_in` order counts normally (the score table does not depend on type).
- Extras only after the core, in spec §11 order.

## Structure (follows the suggested layout in spec §14)

```
package.json            # npm workspaces ["api","web"]; scripts dev / db:setup / test
.nvmrc  .gitignore  docker-compose.yml (exact YAML from spec §9.3)
README.md  DECISIONS.md  CLAUDE.md  docs/  ai-logs/
api/
  .sequelizerc          # points sequelize-cli at src/schema/*
  scripts/wait-for-db.js # db:setup waits for Postgres (clean-machine first boot)
  src/
    app.js              # builds the Express app (routes + error middleware), exported for supertest
    server.js           # app.listen(4000)
    config.js           # env with defaults (DB on 5433, test DB kitchen_queue_test)
    errors.js           # AppError(code, message, details) + code -> HTTP status map
    endpoints/orders.endpoint.js        # HTTP only
    modules/priority.js                 # PURE: PRIORITY_RULES + computeScore(order, now)
    modules/queue.js                    # PURE: ACTIVE_STATUSES, compareQueue (tie-break), rankQueue
    modules/transitions.js              # PURE: TRANSITIONS table, resolveTransition, allowedActions
    modules/orders.module.js            # orchestrates getQueue / transitionOrder (uses the repository)
    repositories/orders.repository.js   # Sequelize: findByStatuses, findById, updateStatusIfCurrent
    schema/config.js  schema/models/*  schema/migrations/*  schema/seeders/*
  tests/fixtures.js
  tests/unit/{priority,queue,transitions}.test.js
  tests/integration/orders.api.test.js
web/
  vite.config.ts        # proxy /orders -> http://localhost:4000 (no CORS needed)
  src/main.tsx  src/App.tsx
  src/api/orders.ts     # fetch + types + ApiError(code)
  src/components/QueueTable.tsx  QueueFilter.tsx  OrderActions.tsx
  src/hooks/useQueue.ts
```

Folders per layer (endpoints / modules / repositories / schema) map 1:1 to the layer table in spec §9.1.

## Design decisions

- **snake_case field names** in the database, models and API JSON — identical to the spec. No translation layer.
- **Priority** — all numbers in `PRIORITY_RULES`; `computeScore(order, now, rules)` is pure (no clock, no Sequelize).
  Input: `{ type, is_vip, placed_at, promised_at, items: [{ prep_time_minutes, quantity }] }`.
  Unknown order type throws. `minutes_waiting` clamped at 0 (clock skew).
- **Queue** — `compareQueue`: score desc → `promised_at` asc (null last) → `placed_at` asc → `id` asc.
  `rankQueue(orders, now)` adds `score`, `wait_minutes`, `allowed_actions`. `ACTIVE_STATUSES` lives here;
  the repository only receives the list and filters. `resolveQueueStatuses` validates `?status=`.
- **Transitions** — `TRANSITIONS = { start: { from: ['received'], to: 'preparing' }, ... }`.
  `allowedActions(status)` is derived from the same table and **sent in the API response**, so the UI
  shows only the buttons the API sends (status rules never duplicated in the UI).
- **orders.module** — `getQueue({ status, now })`; `transitionOrder(id, action)`: load (`ORDER_NOT_FOUND`),
  `resolveTransition`, `updateStatusIfCurrent(id, from, to)`; 0 rows affected (concurrent click) → reload and
  report `INVALID_TRANSITION`.
- **Repository** — returns plain, flattened objects: `items: [{ menu_item_id, name, prep_time_minutes, quantity }]`.
  Conditional update `WHERE id = ? AND status = ?`.
- **Endpoint** — 5 explicit routes; each handler parses the id (`INVALID_ORDER_ID`), calls the module with
  `now = new Date()`, `res.json`. Express 5 forwards rejected promises to the error middleware (no try/catch).
- **Errors** — `{ error: { code, message, details? } }`. `INVALID_ORDER_ID` 400, `INVALID_STATUS_FILTER` 400,
  `ORDER_NOT_FOUND` 404, `ROUTE_NOT_FOUND` 404, `INVALID_TRANSITION` 409, `INTERNAL_ERROR` 500.
- **Schema** — 3 migrations; DB-level NOT NULL / UNIQUE / CHECK / FK constraints; `TIMESTAMPTZ`; index on
  `orders.status` and `order_items.order_id`. STRING + CHECK instead of Postgres ENUM (easy to change). No `sync()`.
- **Seed** — timestamps relative to seed time; fictional English names; rows mapped to each spec §9.5 bullet
  in the seeder header. `db:setup` = wait for DB + undo all + migrate + seed (re-run refreshes the demo).
- **UI** — one page, dense MUI theme (`Table size="small" stickyHeader`; no DataGrid, it re-sorts).
  Columns: score, customer, type, items summary, wait (`wait_minutes` from the API), promised (HH:mm or —),
  VIP chip, status chip, actions. Filter: Active / Received / Preparing. Buttons from `allowed_actions`.
  API errors in a visible `Alert` with code + message. Empty state. Refresh button + last-updated time.
  Reload the queue after each action. No score or ordering logic in the UI.
- **DX** — root: `npm install` · `npm run db:setup` · `npm run dev`. `engines: node 22`. MUI pinned to `^7`.

## Phases (checkpoint with the user after each; every file explained)

0. **Foundation** — done.
1. **Pure rules + unit tests** — done (85 tests).
2. **Schema + seed** — done (constraints verified, clean-machine flow verified).
3. **API** — errors middleware, repository, module, endpoint, app/server; integration tests
   (supertest + `kitchen_queue_test`, created/migrated in Jest setup; close the connection in `afterAll`).
4. **Web** — API client, hook, components, dense theme, proxy.
5. **Docs** — README (prerequisites, 4 commands, ports, error codes), DECISIONS.md (6 sections), `ai-logs/`.
6. **Extras if time allows** — POST /orders (+ validation test) → Vitest → Playwright.

Git: the user makes all commits herself.

## Required tests (spec §10)

  complexity cap; buckets 30m59s→25, 31m→15, 60m59s→15, 61m→0, overdue→25, null→0; delivery VIP with a tight
  promise beats dine_in non-VIP.

## Live-change readiness (goes into DECISIONS.md)

| Likely request | Where it changes |
|---|---|
| Change a weight / cap / bucket | `PRIORITY_RULES` + one test |

2. On screen: order, promised_at tie, caps, ready/terminal orders absent, filters, correct buttons,

3. `curl -X POST localhost:4000/orders/<id>/start` twice → 409 with code.
4. `npm test` green (unit + integration); `npm run test:unit -w api` runs without Docker.
5. Every checklist item in `CLAUDE.md` ticked.

Revisão da API concluída: **121 testes passando** (94 unitários, que rodam sem Docker, e 27 de integração), o linter não acusa nada e as sondagens de ataque agora dão a resposta certa.

## O que encontrei e corrigi

**Segurança e dados**
1. 🔴 **Os testes podiam apagar o banco de desenvolvimento.** Se a variável `DB_NAME` estivesse definida, os testes de integração usariam esse banco e rodariam `TRUNCATE`. Corrigi em duas camadas:
   - o ambiente de teste agora só lê a variável `DB_NAME_TEST`;
   - o próprio teste **se recusa a rodar** num banco cujo nome não termine em `_test`.

   Provei rodando os testes com `DB_NAME=kitchen_queue`: os 10 pedidos do banco de desenvolvimento continuaram lá.
2. 🟠 **URL malformada derrubava em 500.** `POST /orders/%E0%A4%A/start` agora devolve **400 `BAD_REQUEST`**. Esse é um código novo, que vai para a lista do README.
3. 🟡 **Cabeçalho `X-Powered-By: Express` removido.** Era o único aviso de segurança que valia para este projeto. Ferramentas maiores (helmet, CORS, rate limit) seriam exagero para uma ferramenta interna sem login. A falta de autenticação vai para a seção "Next" do `DECISIONS.md`: hoje qualquer um na rede consegue mudar pedidos.

**Bugs e robustez**
4. **Tratador de erros mais correto.** Se a resposta já começou a ser enviada, ele repassa ao Express em vez de tentar responder de novo, que é a recomendação oficial do Express. Todas as respostas de erro agora passam por uma função só (`sendError`), sem montar o JSON em três lugares.
5. **Pedido que some no meio da transição** agora vira 404, em vez de quebrar tentando ler o status de algo inexistente.
6. **A ordem dos itens agora é decidida no SQL** (`ORDER BY`), e não reordenada no JavaScript. Fica mais simples e é o lugar certo, a camada de dados.

**Testes**
7. **Novo `orders.module.test.js`** (6 testes). Com um repository falso, ele **força** o caso "outra requisição mudou o status antes", que o teste de cliques simultâneos não garantia acontecer. Também prova que filtro inválido e transição inválida **nunca chegam a gravar no banco**.
8. Novos testes de integração: URL malformada dá 400, método errado dá 404, cabeçalho `X-Powered-By` ausente. Também corrigi a ordenação numérica num teste: o `.sort()` sem comparador ordenava números como texto.

- **§7**: as 5 rotas, `score` em cada pedido, erros 4xx com código estável.
- **§9.1**: endpoint fino, regras no module, consultas no repository, modelos e migrations no schema.
- **§6**: o servidor recusa transições ilegais, mesmo chamando a API direto.
- **§10**: o pedido cancelado ou retirado sai da fila padrão, provado pela API de verdade.

# CLAUDE.md — Kitchen Display Queue (take-home test)

Full assignment, verbatim: `docs/SPEC.md`. **When in doubt, re-read the spec — it wins over this file.**

## What is being graded (read before every decision)

1. **Organization:** business rules live in the right layer.
2. **Explainability:** the author must explain *every* file and function in a live panel. Prefer simple, obvious code over clever code. No unnecessary dependencies, abstractions or files.
3. **Changeability:** in the panel they will make a **live product change to ranking or status rules**. Changing a weight, bucket, cap, tie-break or transition must be a **one-place edit** (config table / transition map), covered by tests.
4. **Honesty:** 4-hour time box. Smaller + honest `DECISIONS.md` beats wide + unexplainable. Do NOT expand scope.

## Fixed tech stack (do not substitute)

- **API:** Node.js 22, **JavaScript** (not TS), Express, Sequelize 6 **with migrations (never `sync()`)**, PostgreSQL 16, Jest.
- **Web:** Vite, React 19, TypeScript, **MUI 7**, Vitest (extra only).
- **DB:** `docker-compose.yml` with **only** Postgres 16, host port **5433**, user/pass/db = `kitchen_queue` (exact YAML in spec §9.3).
- Ports: API **4000**, web **5173**.
- ⚠️ Local machine has Node 24 (system) + Node 22 via **fnm** (default, PowerShell profile runs `fnm env --use-on-cd`). Always run node/npm under Node 22: in tool shells verify with `node -v`; if it shows v24, prefix with `fnm exec --using=22 -- <cmd>`. `.nvmrc` = 22; also set `engines`. npm latest MUI is 9 → **pin `@mui/material@^7`**. See `docs/RESEARCH.md`.
- One repo, two apps. No private/external repo dependencies.

## API layers (mandatory)

| Layer | Responsibility | Must NOT |
|---|---|---|
| Endpoint | HTTP only: read req, call module, write res. Thin. | contain rules |
| Module | Priority scoring, state machine, queue sorting | touch Sequelize |
| Repository | Sequelize queries, includes, filters | contain rules |
| Schema | Sequelize models + migrations | |

- Priority function is **pure**: `(orderData, now) => number`. Tests run **without Postgres and without mocking Sequelize**.

## Data model

- **MenuItem:** `name` unique non-empty; `category` ∈ starter|main_course|dessert|drink; `prep_time_minutes` int > 0. Seed only, no CRUD.
- **Order:** `customer_name` non-empty; `type` ∈ dine_in|takeout|delivery; `placed_at` set on creation; `promised_at` nullable (relevant for delivery/takeout); `is_vip` bool; `status` ∈ received|preparing|ready|picked_up|cancelled.
- **OrderItem:** `order_id` FK, `menu_item_id` FK, `quantity` int > 0.
- Enforce constraints in the DB too (CHECK / NOT NULL / UNIQUE / FK). Timestamps as `TIMESTAMPTZ`, UTC everywhere.

## Priority score (spec §5)

score = type + vip + wait + promised + complexity

- type: dine_in 30, takeout 20, delivery 10
- vip: +20
- wait: `min(40, floor(minutes_waiting/10)*5)`; `minutes_waiting` = **whole minutes floored** (9m50s → 9 → 0 pts)
- promised: ≤30 min from now → 25; 31–60 → 15; >60 or null → 0
- complexity: `min(20, floor(total_prep/15)*5)`, `total_prep = Σ prep_time_minutes * quantity`
- Tie-break: earlier `promised_at` (null last) → earlier `placed_at` → smaller `id`.
- Computed **at request time**: real clock in app, **frozen `now` injected** in tests. Never `Date.now()` inside the pure function.
- Worked examples A and B (spec §5.3) both = 60, B ranks above A → must be literal test cases.

## State machine (spec §6)

received→preparing, received→cancelled, preparing→ready, ready→picked_up. **Everything else rejected**, including:
skipping steps, repeating same status (start on preparing = error, not silent success), any move from terminal (picked_up, cancelled).
Enforced **on the server** (module), not only by hiding buttons.

## API (spec §7)

| Method | Path | Behavior |
|---|---|---|
| GET | `/orders/queue` | default received+preparing sorted by score; `?status=received\|preparing`; each order includes `score` |
| POST | `/orders/:id/start` | received → preparing |
| POST | `/orders/:id/ready` | preparing → ready |
| POST | `/orders/:id/pickup` | ready → picked_up |
| POST | `/orders/:id/cancel` | received → cancelled |

Errors: 4xx + **stable machine-readable code** (e.g. `INVALID_TRANSITION`, `ORDER_NOT_FOUND`, invalid status filter, invalid id). **Document codes in README.**

## UI (spec §8) — one page, Kitchen Display, MUI, dense ops-dashboard look

- [ ] Table: score, customer name, order type, items summary, wait time, promised time, VIP badge, status
- [ ] Filter: active (default) / received / preparing
- [ ] Only the valid next action per row
- [ ] Cancel for `received` orders
- [ ] Empty state
- [ ] API errors visible on screen (not console)
- [ ] **No scoring formula in the UI**; render rows in exactly the API order

## Seed (spec §9.5)

Dates **relative to UTC now at seed time** (no hard-coded dates). Must demonstrate:
- [x] all 3 types · [x] VIP + non-VIP · [x] wait-time cap (≥80 min waiting) · [x] complexity cap (≥60 prep min)
- [x] score tie broken by `promised_at` (stable ~2 h: same `placed_at`, both promises in the 0-point bucket)
- [x] statuses received, preparing, and ≥1 `ready` (not in active queue)
- Row-by-row mapping lives in the seeder's header comment.

## Required tests (spec §10)

- **Jest priority:** score calc, wait cap, complexity cap, all 4 promised buckets (≤30, 31–60, >60, null), tie-break, lower-base-type-wins case (delivery VIP tight promise beats dine_in non-VIP). **Frozen `now`.**
- **Jest transitions:** every legal transition succeeds; illegal rejected (skip, repeat, from terminal); cancelled/picked_up not in default queue.

## Developer experience (spec §9.4) — README must allow, from a clean machine:

1. `docker compose up -d` 2. one install command 3. one `db:setup` (migrate + seed) 4. one dev command (API + web together)

## Deliverables checklist (spec §12)

- [ ] `README.md`: prerequisites (Docker, Node 22), the 4 commands, ports, API error codes
- [ ] `DECISIONS.md` with sections: **Scope, Layers, Priority, Transitions, AI, Next** (short paragraphs each)
  - Layers: name one rule refused in the UI and why
  - Priority: how score is produced at request time + one easy-to-get-wrong edge case
  - Transitions: where enforced + what happens on start of an already-preparing order
  - AI: one suggestion kept + one rejected/rewritten, **quote the idea**
  - Next: two changes for a real kitchen (not implemented)
  - Note extras attempted/skipped; justify any deviation from suggested layout
- [ ] `ai-logs/` at root with **full** AI conversation exports (Claude Code session `.jsonl` / markdown)
- [ ] API, web, migrations, seed, tests

## Extras (only after core is solid)

1. `POST /orders` (validate items non-empty, menu_item_id exists, quantity positive int, ≥1 Jest validation test)
2. Vitest component test (cancel only for received, or empty state)
3. Playwright happy path with `webServer`, `npm run test:e2e`

## Out of scope — do NOT build

Auth/users/roles, payments, customer entity, pagination, design-system package, Storybook, CI, Restify, Redis, background jobs, WebSockets/real-time, pixel-perfect visuals.

## Decisions taken (record in DECISIONS.md)

- Overdue `promised_at` → 25 pts (the 0 bucket is only "more than 60 min away or null").
- Promise distance in whole floored minutes, like `minutes_waiting`: 0–30 = 25, 31–60 = 15, >60 = 0.
- `promised_at` on dine_in counts normally (the score table does not depend on type).
- `placed_at` in the future (clock skew): wait clamped to 0.
- Unknown order type in `computeScore` throws (no silent 0). Unknown `AppError` code throws.
- Concurrent transitions: conditional UPDATE `WHERE id = ? AND status = from`; 0 rows → `INVALID_TRANSITION`.
- Invalid `?status=` (incl. `ready`, terminal, empty) → 400 `INVALID_STATUS_FILTER`.
- `allowed_actions` sent per order by the API; the UI never re-implements the state machine.
- DB constraints: CHECK instead of ENUM; names must be non-blank (whitespace-only rejected). Migrations and seed run in a transaction.
- `db:setup` = wait for DB + undo all + migrate + seed (repeatable; refreshes demo dates).
- Seed "Example A" placed 30 min ago (spec: 35) so its tie with "Example B" stays stable ~50 min.
- Error codes: BAD_REQUEST 400 (malformed request Express rejects), INVALID_ORDER_ID 400, INVALID_STATUS_FILTER 400, ORDER_NOT_FOUND 404, ROUTE_NOT_FOUND 404, INVALID_TRANSITION 409, INTERNAL_ERROR 500 (cause logged, never sent).
- Clock injected into the app (`createApp({ clock })`) so integration tests freeze time too.
- Test DB isolation: test env uses `DB_NAME_TEST` (never `DB_NAME`) + integration tests refuse a DB not ending in `_test`.
- `x-powered-by` disabled. No CORS (Vite proxy). Known gap for "Next": no auth, so any client on the network can change orders.
- npm audit warnings are dev-only tooling (concurrently, jest); `audit fix --force` would downgrade them.

## Progress

- [x] Phase 0 foundation · [x] Phase 1 pure rules + unit tests · [x] Phase 2 schema + seed · [x] full review
- [x] Phase 3 API + review (121 tests: 94 unit, 27 integration, frozen clock) · [ ] Phase 4 web · [ ] Phase 5 docs/ai-logs · [ ] Phase 6 extras

## Working rules for Claude

- Communicate with the user in Portuguese; code, comments, docs in English. Explain every file created (user must defend it in the panel).
- **Never `git commit`/push** — the user commits herself.
- Any ambiguity → most literal reading of `docs/SPEC.md`. Decisions so far: overdue `promised_at` = 25 pts; promise distance in whole floored minutes (0–30=25, 31–60=15, >60=0); `promised_at` on dine_in counts normally.
- Plan: `docs/PLAN.md`.
- Keep this checklist updated as items are completed.
- Every AI suggestion kept/rejected that is notable → note it for DECISIONS.md "AI" section.

A **tela está pronta e funcionando**. Ela está rodando agora em **http://localhost:5173**, com os dados do seed restaurados. Pode abrir e clicar à vontade.

Testei com um navegador automatizado (Edge), seguindo os itens da seção 8 do SPEC:

| SPEC §8 | Resultado |
|---|---|
| Tabela: score, cliente, tipo, itens, espera, promessa, VIP, status | ✅ |
| Ordem = exatamente a da API | ✅ conferido nome a nome |
| Só a ação válida por status | ✅ botões idênticos ao `allowed_actions` da API |
| Cancelar pedido `received` | ✅ |
| Filtro: ativa / received / preparing | ✅ |
| Tela vazia | ✅ "No orders in this view." |
| Erro da API **visível na tela** | ✅ simulei "outra aba" iniciando o pedido antes; o clique mostrou o alerta com `INVALID_TRANSITION` |
| Visual denso de painel de operação, MUI | ✅ |

## O que cada arquivo faz

- **`api/orders.ts`**: o **único** arquivo que conversa com o servidor. Define os tipos (iguais ao JSON da API) e transforma qualquer falha num `ApiError` com código, inclusive "API fora do ar" (`NETWORK_ERROR`).
- **`hooks/useQueue.ts`**: busca a fila e recarrega quando pedido. Dois cuidados para defender no painel:
  - Se você troca de filtro rápido, uma resposta antiga e lenta **não sobrescreve** a nova (flag `ignore`, padrão da documentação do React).
  - Mantém os dados na tela enquanto recarrega, com uma barrinha de progresso, sem piscar.
- **`components/OrderActions.tsx`**: desenha os botões que a API manda no `allowed_actions`. **Esta é a "regra que você recusou colocar na UI"** do `DECISIONS.md`: a tela não sabe que "received pode ir para preparing". Se mudarem a regra no servidor, a tela se ajusta sozinha.
- **`components/QueueTable.tsx`**: a tabela. Renderiza na ordem recebida, sem ordenar e sem calcular nada.
- **`components/QueueFilter.tsx`**: os três botões de filtro.
- **`format.ts`**: só apresentação (rótulos como "Dine-in", cores dos status, "2× Grilled Salmon"). Nenhuma regra.
- **`theme.ts`**: o visual compacto.
- **`App.tsx`**: a página. Ao clicar numa ação, chama a API e **recarrega a fila em qualquer caso**: se deu erro, a linha passa a mostrar o status real do pedido. No teste, o pedido rejeitado apareceu logo como "Preparing", com o botão "Mark ready".

## Ajuste feito durante a fase
O linter apontou que a primeira versão do hook mudava o estado de dentro do `useEffect` de forma síncrona, o que a documentação atual do React desaconselha. Reescrevi no padrão recomendado: o "carregando" agora é **derivado**, não guardado. Esse é um bom candidato para a seção de IA do `DECISIONS.md`, como exemplo de "sugestão reescrita".

Uma limitação consciente: a fila **não se atualiza sozinha**. O tempo de espera só muda quando você clica em Refresh ou faz uma ação. O SPEC põe atualização em tempo real fora do escopo, então isso vai para a seção "Next".

Próximo passo: **Fase 5**, documentação (`README.md`, `DECISIONS.md` e `ai-logs/`). Quer revisar a tela antes, ou posso seguir?

In the Chip component when variant is set to 'outlined' and color is set to 'warning', the contrast ratio is 3.11:1, which doesn't pass the WCAG 2 AA contrast ratio threshold of 4.5:1. The 'info' color variant also has insufficient contrast at 3.85:1.

The problem specifically affects the outlined variant of the Chip component when using certain semantic color options. Confirmation dialogs should be used before committing to actions with serious consequences — such as destroying users' work or costing large amounts of money, and in particular before actions that cannot be undone. This includes irreversible actions like complete deletion of files (not just to the trash, but forever) or closing an account with all associated information.

## When NOT to Use Confirmation Dialogs

Do not use confirmation dialogs for routine actions. If the user can easily undo an operation, additional confirmation is redundant.

## Best Practices for Dialog Design

For particularly dangerous operations, require a nonstandard action from the user to confirm—rather than simply clicking an OK button, have people do something they would normally not do, such as typing a word into a box.

Try your best to offer undo functionality, a key component of user control and freedom, in order to reduce anxiety and allow users to recover from major problems.

The Nielsen Norman Group's guidance is blunt about the cost of overusing confirmations: cry wolf too often and people stop paying attention, and the dialog loses its power.

I found comprehensive information about data table design best practices. Here's what the search results reveal:

## Right-Alignment for Numbers

Numerical values are much easier to compare and contrast when they're right-aligned. The goal is to align numbers according to the position of the decimal, with all numbers showing the same amount of decimal digits for the most logical display.

## Numeric vs. Qualitative Numbers

Quantitative numbers (amounts, measures, and percentages) should always be right-aligned, while qualitative numbers like dates, zip/postal codes, and phone numbers can be left-aligned.

## Typography for Numbers

It's highly recommended to use a monospace font for numerical values, as it's much easier to scan and compare because all characters are the same size. This avoids problems like $1,111.11 looking visually smaller than $999.99.

## Dense Table Design

Including both horizontal and vertical lines in a grid style provides the most separation between data points, and this spreadsheet-style is recommended for dense, data-heavy tables. Display density can be adjusted with compact (fitting more data), general (balanced spacing), or comfortable (more breathing room) options.

## Avoid Center Alignment

Center alignment prevents quick scanning and noticing irregularities and ultimately makes the eye jump around unnecessarily.

## Enterprise Table Best Practices

Key considerations include keeping the record identifier in column one, making filters visible, aligning numbers right, keeping the header fixed on scroll, and using semantic markup.

Based on the search results, here are the key UX design best practices for kitchen display systems (KDS), particularly for expeditor screens and order priority:

## Readability & Visual Clarity

Your team should be able to read tickets clearly, update progress quickly, and spot priority orders at a glance. Specific recommendations include:

- Large, readable text, clear ticket layouts, simple tap controls, and custom font sizes
- Large, clear fonts and color-coded priorities are essential
- Modifiers and allergy notes should be easy to read at a glance

## Order Priority & Color Coding

Orders are neatly organized with color-coded statuses—a brand-new order might show up in white, one in progress in yellow, and an order that's dragging on too long might flash red—letting a chef scan the line and know exactly where things stand without having to read a single ticket.

KDS tracks how long each order has been active and color-codes tickets based on wait time—an order might start white, turn yellow at five minutes, and go red at ten minutes, providing a visual cue to help kitchen staff prioritize without constantly checking the clock.

## Expeditor Screen Design

The Expo Screen is a display located where the expeditor can see all orders in their entirety—while the system splits the order to various stations, the Expo Screen displays the entire order letting the person in charge of expediting know when each component has been completed.

## Workflow Organization

Effective KDS layouts include order-level view for full ticket tracking, item-level view for station-based prep, grouping for identical dishes, and separate views for dine-in and takeout.

content.text:
Achei a causa das "5 linhas": no banco, **Alice e Emma estão como `ready`**, mudança feita **depois** do meu último seed. Imagino que tenha sido você testando a tela, o que é ótimo. Não é bug: os dois saíram da fila exatamente como deviam. No final eu restauro o seed.

## Avaliação da tela atual

**Medido (auditoria axe-core):**
1. 🔴 **Contraste insuficiente (WCAG AA) nos chips de status.** "Received" tem contraste **3,85:1** e "Preparing" **3,11:1**. O mínimo para texto pequeno é **4,5:1**. É um [problema conhecido das cores padrão do MUI](https://github.com/mui/material-ui/issues/30084). Numa cozinha, com tela distante e luz forte, isso pesa ainda mais.
2. 🟡 **Falta a marcação `<main>`** (landmark). Leitores de tela não acham o conteúdo principal.
3. ✅ A ordem do Tab é lógica: Refresh → filtros → ações.
4. ✅ Em 1280 e 1024 px a tabela cabe inteira. Em 768 px ela rola dentro do próprio quadro, sem quebrar a página. Aceitável para um painel de operação.

**Comparando com as referências:**
5. **Números alinhados à direita.** Score e espera são números para comparar, e o [padrão de tabelas densas](https://www.pencilandpaper.io/articles/ux-pattern-analysis-enterprise-data-tables) é alinhá-los à direita, com dígitos de largura fixa.
6. **Confirmação para cancelar.** Cancelar é **irreversível** (status final). A [Nielsen Norman Group](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/confirmation-dialog/) recomenda confirmar só ações irreversíveis, e só elas, para a confirmação não virar ruído. Os outros botões continuam com um clique.
7. **Retorno de sucesso.** Hoje um clique bem-sucedido não dá nenhum aviso. Um aviso discreto, do tipo "Order #4 → Preparing", resolve.
8. **Promessa relativa.** Em telas de cozinha, [o tempo é o dado central](https://gwenndesign.medium.com/product-design-case-study-kitchen-display-system-52a5e9cab81e). "15:26" obriga o expedidor a fazer conta de cabeça. Mostrar "15:26 · in 20 min" ou "5 min late" (em vermelho) resolve. Para **não** colocar lógica de tempo na tela, a **API** passa a mandar `minutes_until_promised`, calculado com o mesmo "agora" da nota.
9. **Tela vazia por filtro.** "No received orders" é mais claro que uma mensagem genérica.

**Ficam de fora de propósito, por causa do SPEC:**
- Cores por tempo de espera (amarelo aos 5 min, vermelho aos 10), comuns em KDS. Seria uma **regra de negócio na tela**, o que o SPEC proíbe. Vai para "Next".
- Atualização automática: o SPEC põe "real-time updates" fora do escopo.

Começo pela API (o campo novo), com teste.

import { Button, Dialog, DialogActions, DialogContent, DialogContentText, DialogTitle } from '@mui/material'
import type { QueueOrder } from '../api/orders'
import { formatItems } from '../format'

interface ConfirmCancelDialogProps {
  order: QueueOrder | null // null = closed
  onConfirm: (order: QueueOrder) => void
  onClose: () => void
}

/**
 * Cancelling is the only irreversible action (cancelled is terminal), so it alone asks for
 * confirmation; the forward actions stay one click.
 */
export function ConfirmCancelDialog({ order, onConfirm, onClose }: ConfirmCancelDialogProps) {
  return (
    <Dialog open={order !== null} onClose={onClose} aria-labelledby="confirm-cancel-title">
      {order && (
        <>
          <DialogTitle id="confirm-cancel-title">
            Cancel order #{order.id} ({order.customer_name})?
          </DialogTitle>
          <DialogContent>
            <DialogContentText>
              {formatItems(order.items)}. A cancelled order cannot be reopened.
            </DialogContentText>
          </DialogContent>
          <DialogActions>
            <Button onClick={onClose} autoFocus>
              Keep order
            </Button>
            <Button color="error" variant="contained" onClick={() => onConfirm(order)}>
              Cancel order
            </Button>
          </DialogActions>
        </>
      )}
    </Dialog>
  )
}

import { Button, Dialog, DialogActions, DialogContent, DialogContentText, DialogTitle } from '@mui/material'
import type { QueueOrder } from '../api/orders'
import { formatItems } from '../format'

interface ConfirmCancelDialogProps {
  open: boolean
  // Kept separate from `open` so the text stays in place while the dialog fades out.
  order: QueueOrder | null
  onConfirm: (order: QueueOrder) => void
  onClose: () => void
}

/**
 * Cancelling is the only irreversible action (cancelled is terminal), so it alone asks for
 * confirmation; the forward actions stay one click.
 */
export function ConfirmCancelDialog({ open, order, onConfirm, onClose }: ConfirmCancelDialogProps) {
  return (
    <Dialog open={open && order !== null} onClose={onClose} aria-labelledby="confirm-cancel-title">
      {order && (
        <>
          <DialogTitle id="confirm-cancel-title">
            Cancel order #{order.id} ({order.customer_name})?
          </DialogTitle>
          <DialogContent>
            <DialogContentText>
              {formatItems(order.items)}. A cancelled order cannot be reopened.
            </DialogContentText>
          </DialogContent>
          <DialogActions>
            <Button onClick={onClose} autoFocus>
              Keep order
            </Button>
            <Button color="error" variant="contained" onClick={() => onConfirm(order)}>
              Cancel order
            </Button>
          </DialogActions>
        </>
      )}
    </Dialog>
  )
}

content.text:
A revisão completa da tela terminou. Ela está **rodando em http://localhost:5173**, com os dados iniciais restaurados, para você conferir.

## Avaliação: antes → depois

Medi com o **axe-core**, o motor de auditoria de acessibilidade do Lighthouse, e comparei com as referências que pesquisei.

| Ponto | Antes | Depois |
|---|---|---|
| Acessibilidade (axe-core) | 3 violações | **0** |
| Contraste dos status | "Received" 3,85:1 e "Preparing" 3,11:1 (o mínimo é 4,5:1) | cores mais escuras, passam no WCAG AA |
| Tablet (768 px) | nomes quebrados e **botões fora da tela** | nomes inteiros, **coluna de ações fixa** |
| Números | alinhados à esquerda | à direita, com dígitos de largura fixa |
| Promessa | só "15:26" | "15:26 · in 20 min", "in 2 h 59 min" ou "5 min late" em vermelho |
| Cancelar (irreversível) | um clique | **pede confirmação** |
| Retorno de sucesso | nenhum | aviso "Order #4 (Ben Turner) → Preparing" |
| Tela vazia | mensagem genérica | por filtro ("No orders in preparation.") |
| Troca de filtro | linhas do filtro anterior por um instante | nunca mostra linhas erradas |

## Referências usadas
- [Nielsen Norman Group: diálogos de confirmação](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/confirmation-dialog/). Confirmar **só** o que é irreversível, senão a confirmação vira ruído. Por isso "Start" e "Mark ready" continuam com um clique.
- [Pencil & Paper: tabelas de dados empresariais](https://www.pencilandpaper.io/articles/ux-pattern-analysis-enterprise-data-tables). Números à direita, cabeçalho fixo, densidade compacta.
- [MUI issue #30084](https://github.com/mui/material-ui/issues/30084). O problema de contraste das cores padrão do MUI, que a auditoria confirmou aqui.
- [Estudo de caso de tela de cozinha](https://gwenndesign.medium.com/product-design-case-study-kitchen-display-system-52a5e9cab81e) e [boas práticas de KDS](https://www.orderout.co/blog/restaurant-kitchen-display-systems/). O tempo é o dado central, e a leitura precisa ser rápida.

## Fiel ao SPEC
- **A tela continua sem nenhuma lógica de tempo ou de nota.** O "in 20 min" vem de um campo novo da **API** (`minutes_until_promised`), calculado com o mesmo "agora" da nota e coberto por testes. A tela só escreve o número.
- **Ficou de fora de propósito**, e vai para "Next" no `DECISIONS.md`:
  - **Cores por tempo de espera** (amarelo/vermelho), comuns em KDS. Seria regra de negócio na tela, o que o SPEC proíbe.
  - **Atualização automática**: "real-time" está fora do escopo.

## Verificação final
- **124 testes** (eram 121; entraram os do campo novo).
- **Build e linter** limpos.
- **Navegador: 27 de 27 verificações**, cobrindo as seções 5, 6, 7, 8 e 9.5 do SPEC, mais confirmação, aviso de sucesso, alinhamento, API fora do ar e troca de filtro.

Sobre testes automatizados da tela **dentro do repositório**: o SPEC trata isso como **ponto extra**, o teste de componente com Vitest (11.2) e o Playwright de ponta a ponta (11.3). Os testes que rodei agora ficam fora do projeto. Pelo plano, eles entram na Fase 6, depois da documentação.

Quer seguir para a **Fase 5** (`README.md`, `DECISIONS.md` e `ai-logs/`), ou prefere antecipar esses testes da tela?

Based on the search results, here's information about Square KDS order ticket display design, status colors, and timers:

## Status Colors and Timer System

Square KDS uses ticket timers and alerts to prioritize and monitor order status, where orders will appear as yellow or red after a certain amount of time to let kitchen staff know to prioritize that ticket. You can set the times after your Yellow timer and Red timer activate by clicking minutes next to them.

Color coded headers that change from green to yellow to red the longer tickets are open provide a visual indication of how well the kitchen is performing and if any orders are falling behind.

## How It Works

Square takes orders placed on your Square point-of-sale system and automatically displays them on the KDS so your kitchen team can see incoming orders. There's a timer system so you can see how long each order took to complete.

## Customization Features

In the Square KDS app, you can easily customize settings like text size, number of tickets you want displayed, ticket layout, timer options, online order view, and notification options. You can toggle your preferred Ticket layout and number of Columns (4–10), then select your Text size.

## Order Status & Ready Display

Once orders are bumped in Fresh KDS, they move to Ready, and each order card displays the key details including order name, order type (Pickup, delivery, or to-go), and order status such as Received, Ready Soon, or estimated ready time.

## Ticket Color Coding

Fresh KDS helps teams instantly recognize which tickets are new, which have been in the queue for a while, and which are running late through color-coded visual alerts, with on-time orders appearing in green, orders in caution shifting to yellow when they've been in the queue for a set amount of time, and late orders turning red.

## Recall Feature

The Recall feature allows you to instantly restore orders or items to the KDS screen by selecting the order or individual item you need to restore. You can easily recall orders to connected station screens with just two taps.

## Prep-Expo Screen Coordination

The Prep-Expo feature keeps track of completed items on the expo station, with order bumps from station screens automatically striking through items on the expo screen.

I found relevant information about Toast KDS expediter screen ticket layouts. Here are the key findings:

## Toast KDS Expediter Screen Ticket Layout

An expediter shows the entire order in one place and is typically used to call out tickets or assemble plates.

### Ticket Display Elements

At the top of the ticket you'll find the order number and how much time has passed since the order was sent to the kitchen. Every kitchen ticket that appears on a KDS device includes the ticket time, which is a stopwatch-style digital clock, in the upper right corner.

Under the ticket number and time passed you'll find a list of items that are included with the order. The menu item will be listed in black while any and all modifiers will be listed in red.

### Ticket Layout Options

Layout options include Dynamic (uses dynamically-sized tickets that change according to the number of items on the ticket) and Grid (uses a set number of spaces that are used for tickets, with longer tickets able to include multiple spaces).

### Order Type and Time Tracking

A single expediter KDS ticket will include all items for the order. A ticket time is a timer that shows how long ago the order was sent to the kitchen, starting counting at 0:00 when a server sends an order to the kitchen or an online order comes in.

I found several relevant results about order management dashboard UX patterns. Here are the key findings:

## Status Steppers and Progress Display

A status strip placed under the title uses a stepper (like Pending → Confirmed → Shipped → Delivered) plus the next move as one primary button, which provides clear visual hierarchy for order progression.

## Next Action Button Clarity

A NextStep component displays one sentence and one primary action for the order's state, with actions like "Upload," "See comments," or "Copy link" depending on the current state. The next move appears as a single primary button (such as "Confirm order," "Mark as shipped," "Mark as delivered"), while additional actions like "Cancel order" are destructive buttons, and tertiary legal moves go behind a menu.

## Status Column Best Practices

Status badges should use a filled/solid recipe for states like pending, processing, completed, and cancelled, with text labels included so status is not color-only.

## Overall UX Principles

Steppers are UI elements used to display progress and serve navigational purposes that guide users through the next steps of an operation. A horizontal progress tracker with step names and checkmarks gives users full visibility into where they are and what's next.

These patterns emphasize combining clear visual progress indicators (steppers) with explicit, single primary actions to reduce cognitive load and guide users toward the next required step.

# Expediter KDS Ticket Display and Actions

## What the Expediter Sees

The expediter views **one consolidated ticket displaying all order items** regardless of which prep stations handle them. In this example, the expediter ticket shows all three items: Green Tea, Curry Bread, and Ramen.

The ticket layout indicates item status through visual markers:
- **Pending items**: appear without marking
- **Completed items**: display "a green check mark"
- **All items ready**: the "ticket color changes to green"

Items also show their assigned prep station, as the document notes items are "shown on one ticket" with station-level tracking.

## Expediter Actions

The expediter performs a single primary action: **fulfillment upon verification**. Specifically, the expediter "verifies that the items in the order are at the expediter station and fulfills the ticket." Once fulfilled, "the ticket disappears from the expediter KDS device."

## Status Recognition

The expediter knows work is complete when "all items on the expediter KDS device ticket are fulfilled at the prep station level." At that point, visual confirmation arrives automatically—the ticket's color changes to indicate readiness without requiring manual status checks.

content.text:
Pesquisa feita. Antes de mexer, cruzei o que os sistemas reais fazem com cada dúvida sua:

| Sua dúvida | Como os KDS reais resolvem | Fonte |
|---|---|---|
| "O que está acontecendo?" | A tela diz o que é e o resumo do momento (quantos esperando, quantos em preparo) | [Fresh KDS](https://www.fresh.technology/kitchen-display-system) |
| "Qual é o pedido?" | **Número do pedido em destaque** no topo e itens **um por linha**, quantidade primeiro | [Toast: expedidor](https://doc.toasttab.com/doc/platformguide/platformKDSWorkflowUsingSingleExpo.html) |
| "Onde fizeram o pedido?" | Tipo do pedido sempre visível: comer no local, retirada ou entrega | [Fresh: Take-Out View](https://www.fresh.technology/kds-features/take-out-view) |
| "O que já foi feito?" | Etapas concluídas marcadas com ✓ (a Toast usa check verde) | [Toast](https://doc.toasttab.com/doc/platformguide/platformKDSWorkflowUsingSingleExpo.html) |
| "O que é pra clicar?" | **Um botão principal** com o próximo passo escrito por extenso, e cancelar como ação secundária | [padrão de "próximo passo"](https://github.com/amxr21/admin-dashboard/pull/307), [UXPin](https://www.uxpin.com/studio/blog/design-progress-trackers/) |
| "Pra onde foi o pedido pronto?" | Na Toast, o pedido **some da tela** ao ser concluído, igual ao nosso SPEC. Falta só **avisar** | [Toast](https://doc.toasttab.com/doc/platformguide/platformKDSWorkflowUsingSingleExpo.html) |
| Tempo | Cronômetro do pedido em destaque | [Toast: ticket times](https://doc.toasttab.com/doc/platformguide/adminInterpretingTicketTimes.html) |

**Limites do SPEC que mantenho:**
- O SPEC exige **tabela** e visual de painel de operação, então nada de "cartões" como nos KDS. Levo os padrões para dentro da tabela.
- Os pedidos `ready` saem da fila (§5), e a API só filtra received/preparing (§7). Por isso o "pronto" vai virar um **aviso claro** ("pedido #4 pronto, saiu da fila, aguardando retirada").
- **Cores por tempo** (amarelo/vermelho), que todos os KDS usam, continuam de fora: seria regra de negócio na tela.

Vou adicionar os ícones oficiais do MUI (mesma família, versão 7) para os tipos de pedido e as etapas.

import { chromium } from 'playwright-core'

const OUT = process.argv[2]
const browser = await chromium.launch({ channel: 'msedge', headless: true })
const page = await browser.newPage({ viewport: { width: 1440, height: 760 } })
const settle = () =>
  page.waitForFunction(() => getComputedStyle(document.querySelector('.MuiLinearProgress-root')).visibility === 'hidden')

await page.goto('http://localhost:5173')
await page.locator('tbody tr').first().waitFor()
await settle()
await page.screenshot({ path: `${OUT}/v2-overview.png` })

await page.getByRole('button', { name: /^Start preparing: order 1$/ }).click()
await settle()
await page.locator('.MuiSnackbar-root').waitFor()
await page.screenshot({ path: `${OUT}/v2-started.png` })

await page.getByRole('button', { name: /^Mark as ready: order 1$/ }).click()
await settle()
await page.waitForTimeout(300)
await page.screenshot({ path: `${OUT}/v2-ready.png` })

await page.setViewportSize({ width: 1024, height: 760 })
await page.waitForTimeout(300)
await page.screenshot({ path: `${OUT}/v2-1024.png` })
await browser.close()

content.text:
Redesenhei a tela com base em como os sistemas de cozinha de verdade funcionam. Ela já está atualizada em **http://localhost:5173**, com os dados iniciais. Dá uma olhada e me diz se agora faz sentido.

## Suas dúvidas e a resposta na tela nova

| Sua dúvida | O que a tela mostra agora |
|---|---|
| **"O que está acontecendo?"** | Uma frase no topo: *"Orders ranked by priority. Work from the top: start preparing, then mark as ready. Ready orders leave this screen for pickup."* Ao lado do filtro, um resumo: *7 orders · 5 waiting to start · 2 in preparation*. |
| **"O que é pra clicar?"** | A linha 1 tem uma barra azul e o selo **"Next up"**. Cada pedido tem **um botão principal** com o próximo passo por extenso: **"Start preparing"** ou **"Mark as ready"**. "Cancel" fica discreto e pede confirmação. |
| **"O que já foi feito?"** | Uma linha de progresso em cada pedido: **✓ Received — ● Preparing — ○ Ready**. Depois de cada clique, aparece um aviso: *"Order #1 is now being prepared."* |
| **"O pedido já foi feito? Pra onde foi?"** | Ao marcar como pronto: *"Order #1 is ready. It left the kitchen queue and is waiting for pickup."* A Toast funciona assim também: o pedido pronto some da tela do expedidor. |
| **"Onde fizeram o pedido?"** | Ícone e significado em palavras: 🍴 *Dine-in, eats in the restaurant*; 🛍 *Takeout, customer picks up*; 🛵 *Delivery, goes out with a courier*. |
| **"Qual é o pedido?"** | O **número do pedido em destaque** (#1), o nome do cliente com o selo VIP ao lado e **os itens um por linha** (**2×** Grilled Salmon). |
| Tempo | *"1 h 35 min, since 15:15"* e *"17:12, in 19 min"* (ou *"5 min late"* em vermelho). |

Os cabeçalhos com sublinhado pontilhado (Priority, Type, Waiting, Promised) mostram uma explicação ao passar o mouse.

## Referências usadas
- [Toast: fluxo do expedidor](https://doc.toasttab.com/doc/platformguide/platformKDSWorkflowUsingSingleExpo.html): pedido inteiro num lugar, etapas concluídas com ✓, pedido concluído sai da tela.
- [Toast: tempos do ticket](https://doc.toasttab.com/doc/platformguide/adminInterpretingTicketTimes.html): número do pedido e cronômetro em destaque.
- [Fresh KDS](https://www.fresh.technology/kitchen-display-system) e o [modo para viagem](https://www.fresh.technology/kds-features/take-out-view): o tipo do pedido sempre visível.
- [Square KDS](https://squareup.com/help/us/en/article/7944-get-started-with-square-kds-android): leitura rápida e prioridade visível.
- [Padrão de "próximo passo" em telas de pedidos](https://github.com/amxr21/admin-dashboard/pull/307) e [UXPin sobre indicadores de progresso](https://www.uxpin.com/studio/blog/design-progress-trackers/): uma ação principal e a linha de etapas.

## Dentro do SPEC
- Continua sendo **uma tabela** com visual de painel (§8). Mostra nota, cliente, tipo, itens, espera, promessa, selo VIP e status. O VIP passou a ficar ao lado do nome, porque é atributo do cliente.
- A **posição 1, 2, 3…** é só a ordem que a API mandou. A tela não ordena nem calcula nada.
- A linha de progresso é só exibição. **Quem decide os botões continua sendo a API** (`allowed_actions`).
- **Não fiz** cores por tempo de espera, que todo KDS tem, porque seria regra de negócio na tela. Vai para "Next".

## Verificação
- **32 de 32 verificações** do SPEC no navegador.
- **0 problemas** de acessibilidade (axe-core).
- 124 testes, build e linter limpos.
- Cabe inteira em telas de 1280 px. Em tablets, a coluna de botões fica fixa.

O que achou? Se algo ainda estiver confuso, me diga o quê e eu ajusto.

const browser = await chromium.launch({ channel: 'msedge', headless: true })
const page = await browser.newPage()
const requests = []
page.on('request', (r) => r.url().includes('/orders/queue') && requests.push(`${new Date().toISOString().slice(11, 19)} ${r.method()} ${r.url()}`))
page.on('response', async (r) => r.url().includes('/orders/queue') && requests.push(`   -> ${r.status()} ${r.headers()['cache-control'] ?? ''} etag=${r.headers()['etag'] ?? '-'}`))

await page.goto('http://localhost:5173')
await page.locator('tbody tr').first().waitFor()
const updated = () => page.locator('header').innerText()
const refresh = page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Refresh' })
console.log('before:', (await updated()).match(/Updated [\d:]+/)?.[0], '| refresh disabled?', await refresh.isDisabled())
await page.waitForTimeout(2500)
await refresh.click()
await page.waitForTimeout(800)
console.log('after :', (await updated()).match(/Updated [\d:]+/)?.[0], '| refresh disabled?', await refresh.isDisabled())
const firstWait = await page.locator('tbody tr').first().locator('td:nth-child(5)').innerText()
console.log('first row waiting cell:', firstWait.replace(/\s+/g, ' '))
console.log(requests.join('\n'))
await browser.close()

Based on the search results, here's what I found about restaurant order status board and pickup screen design:

## Order Ready Screen Design Overview

An order ready screen is a display that turns the usual pickup chaos into a smooth, organized flow for both customers and delivery drivers. It's like the flight departure board at an airport, but for food.

## Key Design Components

### Status Columns and Layout
Preparing orders are on the left, ready orders are on the right. This two-column layout allows customers to easily distinguish between orders still being prepared and those ready for pickup.

### Essential Features
Real-time status updates display "Preparing" or "Ready" statuses automatically. Screen layout can be configured to customize colors displayed on the screen to indicate order statuses (pending, in preparation, ready for pickup).

### Functional Benefits
Real-time updates like "Order #123 – Being Prepared" and notifications when it's "Ready for Pickup" keep customers in the loop from preparation to completion. When customers can see their order number on a screen moving from "Preparing" to "Ready for Pick-Up," they stop asking staff about their order every 30 seconds.

### Additional Customization Options
Branding and customization features allow you to add your logo, brand colors, and custom layouts to offer a premium customer experience.

Based on the search results, here are the best practices for handling polling with `setInterval` and `fetch` in React with pause functionality when a tab is hidden:

## Key Best Practices

### 1. **Use the Page Visibility API**
Use the `document.hidden` property and the `visibilitychange` event to determine if the page is currently visible or hidden.

### 2. **Create a Custom Hook to Track Visibility**
Monitor visibility changes by creating a hook that listens to the `visibilitychange` event and updates state based on `document.hidden`.

### 3. **Pause Polling When Hidden**
Check if visibility is hidden in the useEffect dependency array—when the tab is hidden, return early to stop the interval; the interval runs only when the tab is visible. This approach makes the interval mount when visible and unmount when hidden.

### 4. **Handle Browser Throttling**
Browsers throttle timers in hidden tabs to roughly once per second, and Chrome drops to once per minute after a tab has been hidden for five minutes, which wastes quota and causes unpredictable polling.

### 5. **Combine Visibility with Other Checks**
Compose visibility tracking with other conditions using `useDocumentVisibility` and `useOnline` by folding them into the delay expression to pause polling in hidden or offline tabs.

### 6. **Consider Refresh on Focus**
Combined with `useDocumentVisibility`, you can pause a poll when hidden and refresh once when refocused — covering both the "long absence" and "quick glance" cases.

## Key Best Practices

### 1. **Use the Page Visibility API**
Use the `document.hidden` property and the `visibilitychange` event to determine if the page is currently visible or hidden.

### 2. **Create a Custom Hook to Track Visibility**
Monitor visibility changes by creating a hook that listens to the `visibilitychange` event and updates state based on `document.hidden`.

### 3. **Pause Polling When Hidden**
Check if visibility is hidden in the useEffect dependency array—when the tab is hidden, return early to stop the interval; the interval runs only when the tab is visible. This approach makes the interval mount when visible and unmount when hidden.

### 4. **Handle Browser Throttling**
Browsers throttle timers in hidden tabs to roughly once per second, and Chrome drops to once per minute after a tab has been hidden for five minutes, which wastes quota and causes unpredictable polling.

### 5. **Combine Visibility with Other Checks**
Compose visibility tracking with other conditions using `useDocumentVisibility` and `useOnline` by folding them into the delay expression to pause polling in hidden or offline tabs.

### 6. **Consider Refresh on Focus**
Combined with `useDocumentVisibility`, you can pause a poll when hidden and refresh once when refocused — covering both the "long absence" and "quick glance" cases.

The general pattern is to make the visibility state a dependency in your polling `useEffect`, returning early if the tab is hidden, which naturally pauses the interval when the component unmounts that effect.

## Modern Operations Dashboard Design Principles

A dashboard UI is effective when it surfaces the right data at the right hierarchy with minimal visual noise.

### Core Layout Patterns

A modern dashboard combines a 256px sidebar that collapses to 64px, a strip of 4-6 KPI cards above the fold, a 12-column CSS Grid with 24px gutters underneath, and row heights of minmax(200px, auto) so panels grow instead of scrolling internally.

### KPI Cards & Stat Cards

Key metric cards should display a large, readable number (the metric), clear label (what it measures), comparison context (vs. last period, vs. target), trend indicator (up/down arrow with percentage), and an optional sparkline (micro-chart showing recent trend).

The shadcn/ui dashboard example shows four KPI cards that pair a number and a trend badge with one line explaining what changed.

### Executive Dashboard Design

Executive dashboard design essentials include 4–6 large KPI cards with trend sparklines; conditional formatting for variance thresholds; single-screen layout requiring no scroll; drill-down available but hidden by default; and minimal chart complexity.

### Information Architecture

Most templates follow a logical flow, with high-level summary metrics (scorecards) at the top and more detailed trend lines, bar charts, and tables below. The layouts are clean and designed for at-a-glance comprehension.

### Clean & Minimal Design

Consistent use of soft-edged cards, a subtle pastel accent palette, and clear typography ensures that even with dozens of data points, the user never feels overwhelmed. This is an ideal benchmark for designers building operational dashboards where speed of data interpretation is the top priority.

These principles reflect the current best practices in dashboard design for 2026, emphasizing clarity, hierarchy, and data-driven decision making.

Based on the search results, here's what I found regarding dashboard auto-refresh, polling intervals, and UX best practices for live data:

## Polling Interval Best Practices

Support recommendation is to set the refresh rate to 5 minutes or more, to match standard polling rates, unless you're polling items at higher frequencies. Setting the interval to 5 seconds provides near-real-time data, while 60 seconds can make a dashboard feel broken.

The larger the dashboard and the more frequent the refresh, the larger the possible impact on resource usage and performance of the web UI.

## When to Avoid Auto-Refresh

Avoid auto-refresh when you can't explain the query cost of each widget, when the dashboard is used by many people at once, or when data changes slowly (daily or weekly) but refresh is set to minutes. The safest default is: don't enable auto refresh until you've sized the load.

## Last Updated Indicator

A 'Last updated' timestamp badge can be added to dashboards, with configurable auto-refresh (Off/30s/1m/5m) and a manual refresh button, using Supabase realtime subscriptions where supported, falling back to interval polling.

## Design Considerations for Real-Time Data

If an endpoint is temporarily unavailable, retain the last-known-good values for that section and mark them clearly as stale/partial/unavailable rather than blanking the whole section. Small animations highlight changes without distracting users—research shows such animations effectively draw attention, with a soft pulse around a changing metric signaling activity without overwhelming the viewer.

content.content:
# Concrete UX Recommendations for Real-Time Dashboards

## Data Freshness & Reliability
- **Data Freshness Indicator**: Implement a compact widget showing sync status, last updated time, and manual refresh button
- **Cached Snapshots**: Display data with timestamps (e.g., "Data as of 10:42 AM") when real-time updates unavailable
- **Skeleton UIs**: Replace spinners with animated placeholders showing expected data structure

## Handling Stale/Unavailable Data
- **Auto-retry with exponential backoff** for connectivity failures before notifying users
- **Clear status banners** like "Offline… Reconnecting…" for transparency
- Maintain user control by preventing unnecessary full-dashboard reloads

## Highlighting Changes
- **Delta indicators and trend sparklines** for at-a-glance value changes
- **Subtle micro-animations** (200-400ms) to draw attention without distraction
- **Directional indicators** (arrows, percentage deltas) paired with color cues for accessibility

## Pausing & User Control
- Offer "snapshot or pause options" so users can process information without continuous updates
- Personalization for alert preferences and update pacing

## Alert Design
- **Binary status indicators** using color (red/orange for critical, green/blue for positive)
- Pair color with icons/labels for accessibility (1 in 12 men are colorblind)
- Use "clear indicators to show if action is required"

## KPI Summaries
- Limit visible elements to ~5 metrics to prevent overload
- Place critical figures in upper left corner per scanning patterns
- Group related data into modular cards with consistent spacing

import DoNotDisturbOnOutlinedIcon from '@mui/icons-material/DoNotDisturbOnOutlined'
import type { Order } from '../api/orders'
import { EMPTY_FINISHED_MESSAGE, formatDuration, formatTime, STATUS_LABEL } from '../format'
import { DurationCell, ItemsCell, OrderCell, TypeCell, VipCell } from './cells'

  { label: 'VIP' },
  { label: 'Type' },
  { label: 'Items' },
  { label: 'Outcome' },
  { label: 'Finished', align: 'right', help: 'When the order was picked up or cancelled.' },
]

/** Recently picked-up or cancelled orders (most recent first, as the API returns them). Read-only. */
export function FinishedTable({ orders, loading }: { orders: Order[] | null; loading: boolean }) {
  return (
    <OrdersTableShell
      label="Finished orders"
      columns={COLUMNS}
      loading={loading}
      isEmpty={orders?.length === 0}
      emptyMessage={EMPTY_FINISHED_MESSAGE}

        <TableRow key={order.id} sx={rowSx}>

          <TableCell>
            <VipCell isVip={order.is_vip} />
          </TableCell>
          <TableCell sx={{ minWidth: 120 }}>
            <TypeCell type={order.type} />
          </TableCell>
          <TableCell sx={{ minWidth: 170 }}>
            <ItemsCell order={order} />
          </TableCell>
          <TableCell>
            {order.status === 'cancelled' ? (
              <Chip icon={<DoNotDisturbOnOutlinedIcon />} label={STATUS_LABEL.cancelled} size="small" variant="outlined" />
            ) : (
              <Chip icon={<CheckCircleOutlineIcon />} label={STATUS_LABEL.picked_up} size="small" color="success" variant="outlined" />
            )}
          </TableCell>
          <TableCell align="right">
            <DurationCell
              minutes={order.minutes_in_status}
              caption={`at ${formatTime(order.status_changed_at)} · ${formatDuration(order.minutes_in_status)} ago`}
            />
          </TableCell>
        </TableRow>
      ))}
    </OrdersTableShell>
  )
}

import { Chip, TableCell, TableRow } from '@mui/material'
import CheckCircleOutlineIcon from '@mui/icons-material/CheckCircleOutline'
import DoNotDisturbOnOutlinedIcon from '@mui/icons-material/DoNotDisturbOnOutlined'
import type { Order } from '../api/orders'
import { EMPTY_FINISHED_MESSAGE, formatDuration, formatTime, STATUS_LABEL } from '../format'
import { DurationCell, ItemsCell, OrderCell, TypeCell, VipCell } from './cells'
import { OrdersTableShell, rowSx } from './OrdersTableShell'
import type { Column } from './OrdersTableShell'

const COLUMNS: Column[] = [
  { label: 'Order' },
  { label: 'VIP' },
  { label: 'Type' },
  { label: 'Items' },
  { label: 'Outcome' },
  { label: 'Finished', align: 'right', help: 'When the order was picked up or cancelled.' },
]

/** Recently picked-up or cancelled orders (most recent first, as the API returns them). Read-only. */
export function FinishedTable({ orders, loading }: { orders: Order[] | null; loading: boolean }) {
  return (
    <OrdersTableShell
      label="Finished orders"
      columns={COLUMNS}
      loading={loading}
      isEmpty={orders?.length === 0}
      emptyMessage={EMPTY_FINISHED_MESSAGE}
    >
      {orders?.map((order) => (
        <TableRow key={order.id} sx={rowSx}>
          <TableCell>
            <OrderCell order={order} />
          </TableCell>
          <TableCell>
            <VipCell isVip={order.is_vip} />
          </TableCell>
          <TableCell sx={{ minWidth: 120 }}>
            <TypeCell type={order.type} />
          </TableCell>
          <TableCell sx={{ minWidth: 170 }}>
            <ItemsCell order={order} />
          </TableCell>
          <TableCell>
            {order.status === 'cancelled' ? (
              <Chip icon={<DoNotDisturbOnOutlinedIcon />} label={STATUS_LABEL.cancelled} size="small" variant="outlined" />
            ) : (
              <Chip icon={<CheckCircleOutlineIcon />} label={STATUS_LABEL.picked_up} size="small" color="success" variant="outlined" />
            )}
          </TableCell>
          <TableCell align="right">
            <DurationCell
              minutes={order.minutes_in_status}
              caption={`at ${formatTime(order.status_changed_at)} · ${formatDuration(order.minutes_in_status)} ago`}
            />
          </TableCell>
        </TableRow>
      ))}
    </OrdersTableShell>
  )
}

import { chromium } from 'playwright-core'

const OUT = process.argv[2]
const browser = await chromium.launch({ channel: 'msedge', headless: true })
const page = await browser.newPage({ viewport: { width: 1440, height: 900 } })
let queueRequests = 0
page.on('request', (r) => r.url().endsWith('/orders/queue') && queueRequests++)

await page.goto('http://localhost:5173')
await page.locator('tbody tr').first().waitFor()
await page.waitForTimeout(600)
await page.screenshot({ path: `${OUT}/v4-queue.png` })

// Time passes by itself: clock ticks every second, data reloads every 15 s without clicks.
const header = () => page.locator('header').innerText()
const clock1 = (await header()).match(/\d{2}:\d{2}:\d{2}/)[0]
const requestsBefore = queueRequests
await page.waitForTimeout(16500)
const clock2 = (await header()).match(/\d{2}:\d{2}:\d{2}/)[0]
console.log(`clock ${clock1} -> ${clock2}; auto reloads of /orders/queue in 16.5 s: ${queueRequests - requestsBefore}`)
console.log('freshness:', (await header()).match(/(Live|Offline)[^\n]*/)?.[0])

// Manual refresh gives visible feedback.
await page.route('**/orders/queue', async (route) => { await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 700)); await route.continue() })
await page.getByRole('button', { name: /Refresh/ }).click()
await page.waitForTimeout(150)
console.log('refresh button while loading:', await page.getByRole('button', { name: /Refresh/ }).innerText())
await page.unroute('**/orders/queue')
await page.waitForTimeout(900)

await page.getByRole('tab', { name: /Ready for pickup/ }).click()
await page.locator('tbody tr').first().waitFor()
await page.waitForTimeout(400)
await page.screenshot({ path: `${OUT}/v4-ready.png` })

await page.getByRole('tab', { name: 'Finished' }).click()
await page.waitForTimeout(800)
await page.screenshot({ path: `${OUT}/v4-finished.png` })
await browser.close()

content.text:
Os cinco pontos estão resolvidos e testados. A tela nova já está em **http://localhost:5173**, com os dados iniciais restaurados.

## Seus pontos

**1. O tempo não passava**
- A tela agora **se atualiza sozinha a cada 15 segundos**. A espera, a promessa e a nota andam sem clique.
- Há um **relógio ao vivo** no canto superior direito.
- A atualização pausa quando a aba fica escondida e atualiza na hora quando você volta.
- Testei: em 16 s sem tocar em nada, a tela recarregou sozinha.

**2. O Refresh "não fazia nada"**
- Ele funcionava, mas não dava retorno: os tempos são em minutos inteiros, então dentro do mesmo minuto nada mudava.
- Agora o botão mostra **"Refreshing…"** enquanto busca, e abaixo do relógio aparece **"● Live · updated 3 s ago"**, com uma bolinha verde pulsando.
- Se a API cair, o indicador vira **"● Offline"** em vermelho.

**3. Ver os pedidos finalizados**
- A tela tem **três abas**:
  - **Kitchen queue**: a fila do SPEC, com o filtro do SPEC.
  - **Ready for pickup**: prontos aguardando o cliente ou o entregador, com o botão **"Mark picked up"**. Antes, esse botão não tinha como ser clicado na tela.
  - **Finished**: retirados e cancelados, do mais recente para o mais antigo.
- Os avisos dizem para onde o pedido foi: *"Order #1 is ready. It moved to 'Ready for pickup'."*

**4. O VIP sumiu**
- Voltou para uma **coluna própria**, com estrela ★. Quem não é VIP aparece com "—", então a coluna nunca parece vazia.

**5. Mais moderno**
- **Cinco cartões de resumo** no topo: esperando, em preparo, prontos, **promessas atrasadas** (em vermelho, com os números dos pedidos) e maior espera. Os três primeiros são clicáveis e levam direto à lista certa.
- Fonte **Inter** (empacotada no app, funciona sem internet), cabeçalho claro, bordas finas e selos com o mesmo estilo nas três abas.

## Dentro do SPEC
- **A fila do SPEC não mudou**: mesma tabela, filtro, ordem e nota vindas da API, e o `GET /orders/queue` intacto.
- As abas novas usam **dois endpoints novos, só de leitura**: `GET /orders/ready` e `GET /orders/finished`.
- O horário de cada mudança de status entrou por uma **migration nova**, sem `sync()`, gravado na mesma instrução que já protege contra cliques duplos.
- A atualização automática é uma **consulta periódica simples**. O §14 do SPEC exclui "real-time updates (WebSockets)", e isso não é WebSocket. Vou registrar a decisão no `DECISIONS.md`.
- Os cartões só **contam e comparam valores que a API mandou**. Nenhuma nota ou ordem é calculada na tela.

## Verificação
- **130 testes** da API passando (eram 124).
- **0 violações** de acessibilidade. A auditoria pegou um texto cinza fraco, que corrigi.
- **39 de 39 verificações** do SPEC no navegador, incluindo o ciclo completo pela tela (received → preparing → ready → picked up), o cancelamento indo para "Finished" e a atualização automática.

Dá uma olhada e me diz o que achou. Se quiser ajustar algo (o intervalo de 15 s, os textos, as cores), é rápido.

Colunas reorganizadas e a identidade visual do cliente aplicada. A tela atualizada está em **http://localhost:5173**, com os dados iniciais.

## Organização das colunas
- **Tudo alinhado à esquerda**, títulos e conteúdo. Cada título fica exatamente em cima do que descreve, sem nada em lados opostos.
- **As mesmas larguras de coluna nas três abas.** Pedido, VIP, tipo e tempos ficam no mesmo lugar em todas.
- **Botões alinhados.** O botão principal tem largura fixa, então "Start preparing", "Mark as ready" e "Mark picked up" ficam um embaixo do outro. O **"Cancel order"** fica sempre logo abaixo, como texto discreto.
- Os títulos com explicação ganham um **ícone ⓘ** padronizado. Passe o mouse para ler.
- **Cabe inteira em 1280 px** (notebook comum), sem esconder etapas nem botões.

## Identidade visual do site deles
Analisei o código do site (HTML, CSS e estilos calculados pelo navegador), não só a aparência:

| Elemento | Site deles | Na nossa tela |
|---|---|---|
| Tecnologia | **Next.js + MUI** | MUI, a mesma biblioteca |
| Fonte | **Nunito Sans** | Nunito Sans (empacotada, licença livre OFL) |
| Fundo de destaque | azul-marinho `#061925` | cabeçalho azul-marinho; selo VIP na cor da marca |
| Cor principal | ciano `#02AACE` | ícone e detalhes do cabeçalho; botões no tom mais profundo `#007C99` |
| Cantos e pesos | 8 px, negrito 700/800 | iguais |

**Uma decisão para você saber, e que vale citar no painel:** o ciano exato deles com texto branco tem contraste **2,75:1**, abaixo do mínimo de acessibilidade (4,5:1). **O próprio site deles falha nisso.** Por isso:
- o ciano original só aparece **sobre o azul-marinho**, onde passa (6,51:1);
- nos botões uso **um tom mais profundo do mesmo ciano** (4,84:1).

Fica com a cara da marca e acessível. Não copiei logo nem nome deles.

## Verificação
- **0 problemas** de acessibilidade.
- **130 testes** da API.
- **Todas as 39 verificações** do SPEC no navegador.
- Build e linter limpos.

# Take-home test: Kitchen Display Queue

> Verbatim copy of the original assignment. Source of truth. Do not edit.

## 1) What this is

Build a small internal tool for a restaurant kitchen. The expeditor (the person who decides what the kitchen works on next) needs a screen that shows every active order ranked by priority, and lets them move each order through its preparation stages.

This exercise is intentionally small. We expect you to use an AI assistant (Cursor, Claude, or similar). We are not grading how much code you can produce. We are grading whether the result is well-organized, whether the business rules live in the right layer, and whether you can explain the decisions you made.

In the technical panel you will walk us through your decisions, and you will change the running code in response to a product request we have not shared here. Design the project so that a change to ranking or to status rules is local and quick.

**Time box:** 4 hours, stop when you hit it. A smaller result with an honest decision log is a better submission than a wide one you cannot explain.

## 2) AI

You may use any AI tool for any part of this exercise.

You must be able to explain every file you submit, including code you did not type yourself. During the panel we will open specific functions and ask why they are written that way. A file you cannot explain works against you.

In `DECISIONS.md`, name one AI suggestion you kept and one you rejected or rewrote. Be specific: quote the idea, not the tool brand.

Include your AI chat logs in the repository. Create a folder called `ai-logs/` at the root and export the full conversation history from the tool you used (screenshots, markdown exports, or .json files — whatever your tool supports). We will not penalize you for wrong turns or failed attempts in the logs; we want to see how you steered the tool, what you asked, and when you course-corrected.

## 3) Domain

A restaurant receives orders throughout the day. Each order has a type (dine-in, takeout, or delivery), a list of menu items, and optionally a promised time. The kitchen does not prepare orders in arrival order; instead, a priority score determines the queue. The expeditor uses this screen to see what to work on next and to advance each order through its stages.

No authentication, no payments, no real customer data.
