- The end-to-end tests run against the development database and reset it to the demo data.

## Layers

**Module** (`api/src/modules`). Every business rule, as plain functions that receive `now` instead of reading the clock: the score (`priority.js`), the queue order and its tie-breaks (`queue.js`), the state machine (`transitions.js`), new-order validation (`new-order.js`), and the use cases that combine them with the repository (`orders.module.js`). Nothing here imports Express, and only the use cases call the repository, so every rule is unit-tested without a database or a mock. This is the [functional core, imperative shell](https://www.destroyallsoftware.com/screencasts/catalog/functional-core-imperative-shell) split: decisions in pure functions, I/O in a thin layer around them.

**Repository** (`api/src/repositories`). Sequelize only: it loads orders with their items, filters by the statuses it is given, creates an order and its lines in one transaction, and moves a status with a conditional `UPDATE ... WHERE status = <expected>`. It makes no decisions. Even which statuses form the active queue is a module rule, passed in as a list.

**Endpoint** (`api/src/endpoints`). Parses the request, reads the clock once per request, calls the module and writes JSON. Every expected error carries a stable code; one table maps codes to HTTP statuses, and one handler writes them.

**UI** (`web/src`). Renders rows in the order the API returns them and turns values into words: status labels, "12 min", "in 20 min". It computes no score and sorts nothing. The one thing it derives is the *Next up* marker: the first row whose allowed actions include `start`.

**The rule I refused to put in the UI: which actions an order allows.** The obvious version is a check in the component, such as "if the status is `received`, show Start and Cancel". That creates a second copy of the state machine, and copies drift. If the server is changed to allow cancelling a `preparing` order, the screen keeps hiding the button. Change it the other way and the screen offers a move the server rejects. The server has to enforce every move anyway, because hiding a button stops no one: as the [OWASP guidance](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.html) puts it, client-side checks are a usability feature and a modified request bypasses them. So the API sends `allowed_actions`, derived from the same `TRANSITIONS` table that enforces each move, and the screen draws one button per action. It is a light form of the [hypermedia controls](https://martinfowler.com/articles/richardsonMaturityModel.html) idea: the response tells the client what it can do next. The server remains the only authority, and allowing a new transition is one edit in one file, with no UI change.

# Decisions

## Scope

I treated the ranking and the status rules as the product, because those are what a kitchen relies on and what is most likely to change. The score weights, the tie-break order and the allowed transitions each live in one table with tests next to it. A product tweak to ranking or status is one edit and one test, and the screen needs no change.

**Built.** The full required core, and all three extras: `POST /orders` with validation and Jest tests for the error cases; a Vitest test for the cancel button (shown only for `received` orders) and the empty state; and a Playwright happy path that starts a seeded order, with `npm run test:e2e` booting what it needs. Every rule in the spec has a test: 166 API tests (unit and integration), 4 component tests and 2 end-to-end tests, all passing, with lint and the type-checked build clean.

**Added beyond the spec, and why.** A *Ready* view and a *Finished* view, backed by read-only `GET /orders/ready` and `GET /orders/finished` and a `status_changed_at` column. Without them, an order marked ready leaves the screen, and the `pickup` transition can only be reached through the API. With each order, the API also sends the actions it allows and the parts of its score, so the screen can explain the ranking without copying the formula or the state machine.

**Left out, and what it costs.**

- No form to create orders: the spec asks for the API only.
- The screen polls every 15 seconds instead of receiving push updates. The expeditor's own actions show immediately; a change made elsewhere can take up to 15 seconds to appear.
- No menu endpoint, so a client calling `POST /orders` has to know the menu item ids.
- The finished list shows the last 20 orders, with no pagination.
- The end-to-end tests run against the development database and reset it to the demo data.

# Decisions

## Scope

I treated the ranking and the status rules as the product, because those are what a kitchen relies on and what is most likely to change. The score weights, the tie-break order and the allowed transitions each live in one table with tests next to it. A product tweak to ranking or status is one edit and one test, and the screen needs no change.

**Built.** The full required core, and all three extras: `POST /orders` with validation and Jest tests for the error cases; a Vitest test for the cancel button (shown only for `received` orders) and the empty state; and a Playwright happy path that starts a seeded order, with `npm run test:e2e` booting what it needs. Every rule in the spec has a test: 166 API tests (unit and integration), 4 component tests and 2 end-to-end tests, all passing, with lint and the type-checked build clean.

**Added beyond the spec, and why.** A *Ready* view and a *Finished* view, backed by read-only `GET /orders/ready` and `GET /orders/finished` and a `status_changed_at` column. Without them, an order marked ready leaves the screen, and the `pickup` transition can only be reached through the API. With each order, the API also sends the actions it allows and the parts of its score, so the screen can explain the ranking without copying the formula or the state machine.

**Left out, and what it costs.**

- No form to create orders: the spec asks for the API only.
- The screen polls every 15 seconds instead of receiving push updates. The expeditor's own actions show immediately; a change made elsewhere can take up to 15 seconds to appear.
- No menu endpoint, so a client calling `POST /orders` has to know the menu item ids.
- The finished list shows the last 20 orders, with no pagination.
- The end-to-end tests run against the development database and reset it to the demo data.

## Layers

**Module** (`api/src/modules`). Every business rule, as plain functions that receive `now` instead of reading the clock: the score (`priority.js`), the queue order and its tie-breaks (`queue.js`), the state machine (`transitions.js`), new-order validation (`new-order.js`), and the use cases that combine them with the repository (`orders.module.js`). Nothing here imports Express, and only the use cases call the repository, so every rule is unit-tested without a database or a mock. This is the [functional core, imperative shell](https://www.destroyallsoftware.com/screencasts/catalog/functional-core-imperative-shell) split: decisions in pure functions, I/O in a thin layer around them.

**Repository** (`api/src/repositories`). Sequelize only: it loads orders with their items, filters by the statuses it is given, creates an order and its lines in one transaction, and moves a status with a conditional `UPDATE ... WHERE status = <expected>`. It makes no decisions. Even which statuses form the active queue is a module rule, passed in as a list.

**Endpoint** (`api/src/endpoints`). Parses the request, reads the clock once per request, calls the module and writes JSON. Every expected error carries a stable code; one table maps codes to HTTP statuses, and one handler writes them.

**UI** (`web/src`). Renders rows in the order the API returns them and turns values into words: status labels, "12 min", "in 20 min". It computes no score and sorts nothing. The one thing it derives is the *Next up* marker: the first row whose allowed actions include `start`.

That creates a second copy of the state machine, and copies drift. If the server is changed to allow cancelling a `preparing` order, the screen keeps hiding the button. Change it the other way and the screen offers a move the server rejects. The server has to enforce every move anyway, because hiding a button stops no one: as the [OWASP guidance](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.html) puts it, client-side checks are a usability feature and a modified request bypasses them. So the API sends `allowed_actions`, derived from the same `TRANSITIONS` table that enforces each move, and the screen draws one button per action. It is a light form of the [hypermedia controls](https://martinfowler.com/articles/richardsonMaturityModel.html) idea: the response tells the client what it can do next. The server remains the only authority, and allowing a new transition is one edit in one file, with no UI change.

Escrevi a seção **Layers** no `DECISIONS.md` depois de conferir cada afirmação no código.

**O que confirmei no código:**
- Os módulos de regra não importam Express e não leem o relógio; o `now` chega de fora, pelo endpoint.
- Só o `orders.module.js` chama o repository.
- A lista de status da fila ativa fica no módulo; o repository só recebe essa lista e filtra.
- Os botões da tela vêm de `allowed_actions`, que sai da mesma tabela `TRANSITIONS` que valida as mudanças de status.
- A UI não ordena nada nem calcula o score: só mostra o número que vem da API.

**Uma correção no rascunho:** eu tinha escrito que erros de qualquer camada viram código HTTP, mas o repository não lança erro de regra. Agora o texto diz: "uma tabela mapeia códigos para HTTP e um handler escreve a resposta".

**Fundamentos da pesquisa (uma frase cada, com link):**

| Decisão nossa | Fundamento citado |
|---|---|
| Regras em funções puras, com `now` vindo de fora | *Functional Core, Imperative Shell*, de Gary Bernhardt |
| Toda mudança de status é validada no servidor, mesmo com o botão escondido | Cheat sheet de autorização da OWASP |
| A API envia `allowed_actions` para a tela | *Hypermedia controls*, nível 3 do Richardson Maturity Model, de Martin Fowler |

Os três links abrem. Também li o texto da OWASP: ele diz que checagens no cliente *"may be permissible for improving the user experience"*, mas *"client-side logic is often easy to bypass"*. A minha frase dizia mais do que isso, então reescrevi para ficar fiel ao original.

Na banca, se perguntarem "por que mandar `allowed_actions`?", você tem duas respostas: a prática (cópias da regra se desencontram) e a de segurança (OWASP). O Fowler mostra que é um padrão conhecido de API, não invenção nossa.

Próxima seção: **Priority**. O spec pede como o score é calculado na hora da requisição e um caso de borda fácil de errar. Faço do mesmo jeito: confiro no código, pesquiso e escrevo?

Fontes:
- [Functional Core, Imperative Shell, Destroy All Software](https://www.destroyallsoftware.com/screencasts/catalog/functional-core-imperative-shell)
- [OWASP Authorization Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.html)
- [Richardson Maturity Model, Martin Fowler](https://martinfowler.com/articles/richardsonMaturityModel.html)

> *"What lives in the module, the repository, and the UI. **Name one rule you refused to put in the UI and why**"*

"Refused to put **in the UI**" quer dizer: uma regra que eu poderia ter duplicado na tela e escolhi deixar **só no servidor**. A regra existe e funciona:

- **Onde ela está:** a tabela `TRANSITIONS` em `api/src/modules/transitions.js` define quais ações cada status permite.
- **O que a API faz:** recusa qualquer movimento ilegal com `409 INVALID_TRANSITION` e manda para a tela a lista `allowed_actions` de cada pedido.
- **O que a tela faz:** só desenha os botões dessa lista. Ela não tem um `if (status === 'received')` próprio, porque seria uma segunda cópia da regra.

Dito isso, se a frase te confundiu, pode confundir o avaliador também. Posso trocar o título para algo mais explícito, por exemplo:

> **The rule I kept on the server and out of the UI: which actions an order allows.**

Assim fica claro já no título que a regra existe e onde ela mora. Troco?

The kitchen does not prepare orders in arrival order; instead, a priority score determines the queue. The expeditor uses this screen to see what to work on next and to advance each order through its stages.

48:| `promised_at` | Timestamp or null. Relevant for `delivery` and `takeout`. |
64:Sort by priority score, highest first. The score is computed at request time, using the real clock in the running app and a frozen `now` in tests. All time comparisons use UTC.
66:### 5.1) Score
74:| Wait time | `min(40, floor(minutes_waiting / 10) * 5)` | |
75:| Promised time | `promised_at` is within 30 minutes from now | 25 |
76:| | `promised_at` is within 31–60 minutes from now | 15 |
77:| | `promised_at` is more than 60 minutes away or null | 0 |
78:| Complexity | `min(20, floor(total_prep_minutes / 15) * 5)` | |

83:- `total_prep_minutes` = sum of (`prep_time_minutes * quantity`) across all items in the order;
87:When two orders have the same score, sort by:

106:| Promised | null | 0 |

## Priority

**Produced at request time, never stored.** The endpoint reads the clock once per request and passes that `now` down. The module loads the active orders, scores every one of them against the same `now`, and sorts them in memory with the tie-break list in `QUEUE_ORDER`. One instant per response means the score, the waiting time and the "promised in" shown on a row always agree with each other. The score is not a column because it depends on the clock: a stored score is wrong a minute later and would need a background job to keep it fresh. Computing it in SQL would make a second copy of the formula. The cost is loading every active order on each request, which is fine for a kitchen with a few dozen open orders.

The weights, caps and promise buckets live in `PRIORITY_RULES`. `scoreBreakdown` returns the points of each part and `computeScore` is their sum, so the score and the explanation on screen cannot disagree. The clock is injected through `createApp({ clock })`: the running app uses the real time and the tests a frozen `2026-06-15T12:00:00Z`. This is the approach the [Java time API documents as best practice](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/time/Clock.html): pass a clock to any code that needs the current instant, so tests can use a fixed one.

**The edge case that was easy to get wrong: the promise buckets.** The spec gives 25 points "within 30 minutes", 15 "within 31–60 minutes", and 0 for "more than 60 minutes away or null". Read naively, this has two holes:

- **A gap between buckets.** With seconds precision, a promise 30 minutes 30 seconds away is neither within 30 nor within 31–60, and falls through to 0. I measure it in whole floored minutes, the same rule the spec sets for `minutes_waiting`. The buckets then have no gap: 30m59s is 30 minutes and scores 25, 31 minutes scores 15.
- **An overdue promise.** The spec does not list it. A check such as `minutes >= 0 && minutes <= 30` gives a late order 0 points, so it drops in the queue exactly when it should go first. On the literal reading, only "more than 60 minutes away or null" scores 0, and an overdue promise is within 30 minutes, so it scores 25.

Both boundaries are tests: 30m59s, 31m, 60m59s, 61m, due now, and 10 minutes overdue. If the kitchen wants late orders boosted even more, that is a new bucket in `PRIORITY_RULES`.
EOF
tail -3 DECISIONS.md

Escrevi a seção **Priority** no `DECISIONS.md`, com tudo conferido no código.

**Como o score é calculado na hora:**
- O endpoint lê o relógio uma vez por requisição e todos os pedidos da resposta são calculados com esse mesmo instante. Assim o score, o tempo de espera e o "promised in" de cada linha nunca se contradizem.
- Explico por que o score não é uma coluna no banco: ele depende do relógio, então um minuto depois estaria errado e precisaria de um job para atualizar. E por que não é calculado em SQL: seria uma segunda cópia da fórmula.
- Assumo o custo: a API carrega todos os pedidos ativos a cada requisição, o que não pesa para uma cozinha com algumas dezenas de pedidos abertos.
- Fundamento citado: a documentação oficial do Java recomenda passar o relógio para quem precisa do horário atual, para os testes poderem usar um horário fixo. Conferi a citação no texto original.

**Caso de borda: as faixas de prazo prometido (`promised_at`).** O spec deixa dois buracos:
- **Entre 30 e 31 minutos.** Contando segundos, um prazo a 30 min 30 s não cai em "até 30" nem em "31 a 60", e acabaria com 0 pontos. Resolvi contando minutos inteiros arredondados para baixo, a mesma regra que o spec usa para o tempo de espera.
- **Prazo já vencido.** O spec não cita esse caso. Uma checagem ingênua daria 0 pontos ao pedido atrasado, que cairia na fila justamente quando mais precisa subir. Pela leitura literal do spec, ele fica com 25.

Os dois casos têm teste. No fim da seção, deixei uma frase que prepara a mudança ao vivo na banca: se a cozinha quiser dar ainda mais prioridade aos atrasados, basta uma nova faixa no `PRIORITY_RULES`. Conferi que funciona: uma faixa `{ upToMinutes: -1, … }` colocada antes das outras pega só os pedidos vencidos.

Próxima seção: **Transitions**. O spec pergunta onde a máquina de estados é validada e o que acontece ao dar *start* num pedido que já está `preparing`. Sigo do mesmo jeito.

# Decisions

## Scope

I treated the ranking and the status rules as the product, because those are what a kitchen relies on and what is most likely to change. The score weights, the tie-break order and the allowed transitions each live in one table with tests next to it. A product tweak to ranking or status is one edit and one test, and the screen needs no change.

**Built.** The full required core, and all three extras: `POST /orders` with validation and Jest tests for the error cases; a Vitest test for the cancel button (shown only for `received` orders) and the empty state; and a Playwright happy path that starts a seeded order, with `npm run test:e2e` booting what it needs. Every rule in the spec has a test: 166 API tests (unit and integration), 4 component tests and 2 end-to-end tests, all passing, with lint and the type-checked build clean.

**Added beyond the spec, and why.** A *Ready* view and a *Finished* view, backed by read-only `GET /orders/ready` and `GET /orders/finished` and a `status_changed_at` column. Without them, an order marked ready leaves the screen, and the `pickup` transition can only be reached through the API. With each order, the API also sends the actions it allows and the parts of its score, so the screen can explain the ranking without copying the formula or the state machine.

**Left out, and what it costs.**

- No form to create orders: the spec asks for the API only.
- The screen polls every 15 seconds instead of receiving push updates. The expeditor's own actions show immediately; a change made elsewhere can take up to 15 seconds to appear.
- No menu endpoint, so a client calling `POST /orders` has to know the menu item ids.
- The finished list shows the last 20 orders, with no pagination.
- The end-to-end tests run against the development database and reset it to the demo data.

## Layers

**Module** (`api/src/modules`). Every business rule, as plain functions that receive `now` instead of reading the clock: the score (`priority.js`), the queue order and its tie-breaks (`queue.js`), the state machine (`transitions.js`), new-order validation (`new-order.js`), and the use cases that combine them with the repository (`orders.module.js`). Nothing here imports Express, and only the use cases call the repository, so every rule is unit-tested without a database or a mock. This is the [functional core, imperative shell](https://www.destroyallsoftware.com/screencasts/catalog/functional-core-imperative-shell) split: decisions in pure functions, I/O in a thin layer around them.

**Repository** (`api/src/repositories`). Sequelize only: it loads orders with their items, filters by the statuses it is given, creates an order and its lines in one transaction, and moves a status with a conditional `UPDATE ... WHERE status = <expected>`. It makes no decisions. Even which statuses form the active queue is a module rule, passed in as a list.

**Endpoint** (`api/src/endpoints`). Parses the request, reads the clock once per request, calls the module and writes JSON. Every expected error carries a stable code; one table maps codes to HTTP statuses, and one handler writes them.

**UI** (`web/src`). Renders rows in the order the API returns them and turns values into words: status labels, "12 min", "in 20 min". It computes no score and sorts nothing. The one thing it derives is the *Next up* marker: the first row whose allowed actions include `start`.

**The rule I kept on the server and out of the UI: which actions an order allows.** The obvious version is a check in the component, such as "if the status is `received`, show Start and Cancel". That creates a second copy of the state machine, and copies drift. If the server is changed to allow cancelling a `preparing` order, the screen keeps hiding the button. Change it the other way and the screen offers a move the server rejects. The server has to enforce every move anyway, because hiding a button stops no one: as the [OWASP guidance](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.html) puts it, client-side checks may improve the user experience but must never be the deciding factor, because client-side logic is easy to bypass. So the API sends `allowed_actions`, derived from the same `TRANSITIONS` table that enforces each move, and the screen draws one button per action. It is a light form of the [hypermedia controls](https://martinfowler.com/articles/richardsonMaturityModel.html) idea: the response tells the client what it can do next. The server remains the only authority, and allowing a new transition is one edit in one file, with no UI change.

## Priority

**Produced at request time, never stored.** The endpoint reads the clock once per request and passes that `now` down. The module loads the active orders, scores every one of them against the same `now`, and sorts them in memory with the tie-break list in `QUEUE_ORDER`. One instant per response means the score, the waiting time and the "promised in" shown on a row always agree with each other. The score is not a column because it depends on the clock: a stored score is wrong a minute later and would need a background job to keep it fresh. Computing it in SQL would make a second copy of the formula. The cost is loading every active order on each request, which is fine for a kitchen with a few dozen open orders.

The weights, caps and promise buckets live in `PRIORITY_RULES`. `scoreBreakdown` returns the points of each part and `computeScore` is their sum, so the score and the explanation on screen cannot disagree. The clock is injected through `createApp({ clock })`: the running app uses the real time and the tests a frozen `2026-06-15T12:00:00Z`. This is the approach the [Java time API documents as best practice](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/time/Clock.html): pass a clock to any code that needs the current instant, so tests can use a fixed one.

**The edge case that was easy to get wrong: the promise buckets.** The spec gives 25 points "within 30 minutes", 15 "within 31–60 minutes", and 0 for "more than 60 minutes away or null". Read naively, this has two holes:

- **A gap between buckets.** With seconds precision, a promise 30 minutes 30 seconds away is neither within 30 nor within 31–60, and falls through to 0. I measure it in whole floored minutes, the same rule the spec sets for `minutes_waiting`. The buckets then have no gap: 30m59s is 30 minutes and scores 25, 31 minutes scores 15.
- **An overdue promise.** The spec does not list it. A check such as `minutes >= 0 && minutes <= 30` gives a late order 0 points, so it drops in the queue exactly when it should go first. On the literal reading, only "more than 60 minutes away or null" scores 0, and an overdue promise is within 30 minutes, so it scores 25.

Both boundaries are tests: 30m59s, 31m, 60m59s, 61m, due now, and 10 minutes overdue. If the kitchen wants late orders boosted even more, that is a new bucket in `PRIORITY_RULES`.

**Enforced in the module, in one table.** `TRANSITIONS` in `api/src/modules/transitions.js` lists each action, the statuses it may start from, and the status it leads to. An integration test fires two starts at once and expects exactly one `200` and one `409`.

**Starting an order that is already `preparing`.** The API answers `409` and writes nothing: the status and `status_changed_at` stay as they were.

```json
    "code": "INVALID_TRANSITION",
    "message": "Cannot start an order that is preparing.",
    "details": { "action": "start", "current_status": "preparing", "allowed_from": ["received"] }
  }
}
```

EOF

content.text:
A seção **Transitions** está escrita no `DECISIONS.md`. Conferi no código e nos testes tudo o que ela afirma.

**Onde a máquina de estados é validada.** Na tabela `TRANSITIONS`, dentro do módulo. O clique na tela e a chamada direta à API passam pela mesma checagem. O teste unitário cobre os 20 pares de status × ação: as 4 mudanças permitidas passam e as 16 ilegais são recusadas.

**Dois cliques ao mesmo tempo.** O `UPDATE ... WHERE status = <status lido>` impede que os dois cliques sejam aceitos. Citei o padrão *Optimistic Offline Lock* do Fowler, e um teste de integração dispara os dois cliques juntos e espera exatamente uma resposta 200 e uma 409.

**Start num pedido que já está `preparing`.** A API responde 409, mostrado com o JSON real, e não grava nada. A seção justifica a escolha de três jeitos:
- pelo RFC 9110, com o texto exato copiado da fonte;
- pelo spec, que diz que repetir uma transição é erro;
- por um argumento de cozinha: um segundo *Start* geralmente significa duas pessoas no mesmo pedido, e alguém precisa saber disso.

A seção também diz o que a tela faz: mostra um alerta vermelho com a mensagem e o código, e atualiza a fila.

---

**AI** é a única seção que não dá para eu escrever sozinho. Ela precisa bater com os logs da nossa conversa e com as decisões que *você* tomou. Proponho:

> ## AI
>
> **Kept: "two clicks can both pass the status check; write with a conditional `UPDATE ... WHERE status = <expected>` and treat zero affected rows as a conflict."** The spec does not mention concurrency, and my first version read the order, checked the move and saved it. The suggestion was right: two expeditors pressing *Start* together would both succeed. I kept it because the fix is one condition in one query, with no locks, and I asked for a test that proves it by firing two requests at once.
>
> **Rewritten: "build the score explanation in the priority module, returning lines such as 'Dine-in: +30 pts' and the formula text, so the tooltip can show how the score was computed."** I rejected two things in it. Presentation text inside the rule module mixes layers: rewording a tooltip would mean editing the scoring code. And per-row arithmetic on screen comes close to the second copy of the formula that the spec forbids in the UI. I rewrote it so the module returns only numbers (`score_breakdown`), and the screen turns the non-zero parts into plain reasons, such as "VIP customer" or "promised soon", without points.

Duas coisas para você conferir:

- **A frase "my first version read the order, checked the move and saved it" é verdadeira?** O UPDATE condicional já estava no plano desde o início, então talvez a sugestão tenha vindo antes de existir código. Se for o caso, troco por *"the plan I started from read, checked and saved"*, ou escolho outra sugestão aceita. Também poderia ser o relógio injetado, ou os minutos inteiros nas faixas de prazo.
- **A recusa** foi decisão sua ("acho que não precisa dos números... é só algum ser humano fazer uma conta de soma"), então ela é autêntica nos logs. Quer que eu mencione que a sugestão original chegou a ir para a tela antes de você cortar? Isso mostra que você corrigiu o rumo da IA, e é exatamente o que o spec diz querer ver nos logs.

- [RFC 9110 §15.5.10, 409 Conflict](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#name-409-conflict)

# CLAUDE.md

Project guide for AI assistants working in this repository. The assignment, verbatim, is in
`docs/SPEC.md` and always takes precedence over this file.

## Working rules

- Talk to the user in Portuguese; write code, comments and docs in English.
- Never commit or push; the user handles git.
- Never state in any file that the time box was exceeded.
- Resolve ambiguities with the most literal reading of the spec.
- Keep comments short and only where the reason is not obvious.
- Run everything under Node 22 (`.nvmrc`). The machine also has Node 24; if `node -v` shows v24,
  prefix commands with `fnm exec --using=22 --`.

## Stack (fixed by the spec)

- API: Node 22, JavaScript, Express 5, Sequelize 6 with migrations (never `sync()`), PostgreSQL 16, Jest.
- Web: Vite, React 19, TypeScript, MUI 7 (pinned: npm's latest is 9).
- `docker-compose.yml`: Postgres 16 only, host port 5433. API on 4000, web on 5173.

## Layout

```
api/src/endpoints      HTTP only (routes, error handler)
api/src/modules        rules: priority.js, queue.js, transitions.js, orders.module.js
api/src/repositories   Sequelize queries
api/src/schema         models, migrations, seeders, sequelize-cli config
api/tests              unit (no database) and integration (supertest + kitchen_queue_test)
web/src                api client, hooks, components, format.ts (labels), theme.ts
```

## Where product changes go

| Change | Place |
|---|---|
| Score weights, caps, promise buckets | `PRIORITY_RULES` in `api/src/modules/priority.js` |
| Tie-break order or a new tie-break | `QUEUE_ORDER` in `api/src/modules/queue.js` |
| Allowed status transitions | `TRANSITIONS` in `api/src/modules/transitions.js` |
| A new status | migration updating the `orders_status_valid` CHECK, then `TRANSITIONS` |

The UI renders unknown statuses, types, actions and tie-breaks with readable fallbacks
(`format.ts`), so server-side changes do not require UI changes.

## Decisions in effect

- Promise distance uses whole floored minutes (0-30 = 25, 31-60 = 15); an overdue promise scores 25.
- `promised_at` on a dine-in order counts like any other promise.
- `minutes_waiting` is clamped at 0 (clock skew). An order type without a weight throws.
- Transitions use a conditional `UPDATE ... WHERE status = <from>`; a lost race returns `INVALID_TRANSITION`.
- The API sends `allowed_actions`, `score_breakdown` and `ahead_of_next` with each order; the UI never
  re-implements the state machine or the formula. The score is shown in the table (required).
- Read-only extensions: `GET /orders/ready`, `GET /orders/finished`, column `status_changed_at`.
- The UI polls every 15 s (paused while the tab is hidden); no push channel.
- Tests use a frozen clock; the test database is isolated (`DB_NAME_TEST`, `*_test` guard).
- `db:setup` waits for Postgres, resets the schema and reseeds with dates relative to now.

## Commands

```
docker compose up -d
npm install
npm run db:setup
npm run dev          # API + web
npm test             # API unit + integration (needs Docker), then web Vitest
npm run test:e2e     # Playwright (resets the demo data first)
npm run lint
npm run build
```

## Pending

- `DECISIONS.md` (spec sections, written with the user), `ai-logs/`.

- Promise distance uses whole floored minutes (0-30 = 25, 31-60 = 15); an overdue promise scores 25.
- `promised_at` on a dine-in order counts like any other promise.

- Tests use a frozen clock; the test database is isolated (`DB_NAME_TEST`, `*_test` guard).
- `db:setup` waits for Postgres, resets the schema and reseeds with dates relative to now.

# Idempotent requests

Read this page in your terminal: [install the Stripe CLI](https://docs.stripe.com/cli/install) (v1.43.3+) and run `stripe docs`. [Reference](https://docs.stripe.com/cli/docs)

## Start here: Integrate with Stripe using skills and plugins

Stripe provides skills and plugins for agents to build faster and more accurately. See [Agent skills](https://docs.stripe.com/skills.md) for more information.

**Quickstart**: Install the Stripe CLI with `npm install -g @stripe/cli` and run `stripe agent setup`.

> Nested parameters, fields, and event types on API reference pages are collapsed by default. Use the provided `?query=<name>` links to show the full definitions. Request the page with an empty `?query=` to expand every entry at once.

```sh
curl https://api.stripe.com/v1/customers \
  -u [example key removed]: \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: KG5LxwFBepaKHyUD" \
  -d description="My First Test Customer (created for API docs at https://docs.stripe.com/api)"
```

The API supports [idempotency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idempotence) for safely retrying requests without accidentally performing the same operation twice. When creating or updating an object, use an idempotency key. Then, if a connection error occurs, you can safely repeat the request without risk of creating a second object or performing the update twice.

To perform an idempotent request, provide an additional `IdempotencyKey` element to the request options.

Stripe’s idempotency works by saving the resulting status code and body of the first request made for any given idempotency key, regardless of whether it succeeds or fails. Subsequent requests with the same key return the same result, including `500` errors.

A client generates an idempotency key, which is a unique key that the server uses to recognize subsequent retries of the same request. How you create unique keys is up to you, but we suggest using V4 UUIDs, or another random string with enough entropy to avoid collisions. Idempotency keys are up to 255 characters long. Avoid using sensitive data (for example, email addresses or personal identifiers) as idempotency keys.

You can remove keys from the system automatically after they’re at least 24 hours old. We generate a new request if a key is reused after the original is pruned. The idempotency layer compares incoming parameters to those of the original request and errors if they’re not the same to prevent accidental misuse.

We save results only after the execution of an endpoint begins. If incoming parameters fail validation, or the request conflicts with another request that’s executing concurrently, we don’t save the idempotent result because no API endpoint initiates the execution. You can retry these requests. Learn more about when you can [retry idempotent requests](https://docs.stripe.com/error-low-level.md#idempotency).

All `POST` requests accept idempotency keys. Don’t send idempotency keys in `GET` and `DELETE` requests because it has no effect. These requests are idempotent by definition.

cat >> DECISIONS.md <<'EOF'

## AI

**Kept: "Concurrent transitions (two clicks on start): conditional UPDATE `WHERE status = from` / row lock."** This came up while analysing the spec, before any code existed, as one of the edge cases the spec does not mention. A read, check and save would let two expeditors start the same order. I kept the conditional `UPDATE` and dropped the row lock: one query, no lock held across requests, and a lost race comes back as the same `INVALID_TRANSITION` the client already handles. It is described under *Transitions* and covered by a test that fires two starts at once.

**Rewritten: a score explanation built inside the priority module.** The first version of `scoreBreakdown` returned, for each part of the score, `{ component, label, formula, points }`, with display strings such as `` `VIP +${rules.vipPoints}` `` and `` `${prep} min of total prep time` ``, and the tooltip on screen showed them with their points. I rejected it for two reasons. Display text inside the rule module mixes layers: rewording a tooltip would mean editing the scoring code. And with the points on every row, anyone can add them up, so the screen effectively carries the formula, which is what the spec says the UI must not contain. I rewrote it so the module returns only numbers (`score_breakdown`), and the screen turns the parts that count into plain reasons, such as "VIP customer" or "promised soon", with no points.

## Next

**1. Staff sign-in and a status history.** Today anyone who can reach the screen can move any order, and only the latest status change is kept. In a real kitchen, a mis-click on *Mark ready* sends a cook's order to the pass with no trace of who did it and no way back. I would add sign-in per station and an `order_status_events` table (order, from, to, who, when), written in the same transaction as the conditional update. That gives the manager an audit trail and makes a safe *undo* possible, through a new entry in `TRANSITIONS` that only some roles may use.

**2. Safe order intake from the point of sale.** Orders would arrive from the till and delivery platforms through `POST /orders`, which today is open and not retry-safe. A network timeout followed by a retry creates the same ticket twice, and the kitchen cooks it twice. I would require an API key per source and an `Idempotency-Key` header: the server stores the result of the first request for each key and returns it for any retry, as [Stripe's API does](https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests) and as the [IETF draft](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-httpapi-idempotency-key-header/) standardises.

I would not start with push updates. Polling every 15 seconds is enough to see what to cook next, and a screen that is behind is already safe: an action on an order that moved elsewhere is rejected and the screen refreshes.
EOF

lines: I chose `409` because [RFC 9110](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#name-409-conflict) defines it for a request that "could not be completed due to a conflict with the current state of the target resource", which is exactly this case. A silent `200` would be easier, but the spec calls a repeated transition an error, and in a kitchen a second *Start* usually means two people are working the same ticket, which someone should know about. On screen, the error appears in a red alert with the message and the code. The queue refreshes at the same time, so the row shows the order's real status.

+**Kept: "Concurrent transitions (two clicks on start): conditional UPDATE `WHERE status = from` / row lock."** This came up while analysing the spec, before any code existed, as one of the edge cases the spec does not mention. A read, check and save would let two expeditors start the same order. I kept the conditional `UPDATE` and dropped the row lock: one query, no lock held across requests, and a lost race comes back as the same `INVALID_TRANSITION` the client already handles. It is described under *Transitions* and covered by a test that fires two starts at once.

+**Rewritten: a score explanation built inside the priority module.** The first version of `scoreBreakdown` returned, for each part of the score, `{ component, label, formula, points }`, with display strings such as `` `VIP +${rules.vipPoints}` `` and `` `${prep} min of total prep time` ``, and the tooltip on screen showed them with their points. I rejected it for two reasons. Display text inside the rule module mixes layers: rewording a tooltip would mean editing the scoring code. And with the points on every row, anyone can add them up, so the screen effectively carries the formula, which is what the spec says the UI must not contain. I rewrote it so the module returns only numbers (`score_breakdown`), and the screen turns the parts that count into plain reasons, such as "VIP customer" or "promised soon", with no points.

+**1. Staff sign-in and a status history.** Today anyone who can reach the screen can move any order, and only the latest status change is kept. In a real kitchen, a mis-click on *Mark ready* sends a cook's order to the pass with no trace of who did it and no way back. I would add sign-in per station and an `order_status_events` table (order, from, to, who, when), written in the same transaction as the conditional update. That gives the manager an audit trail and makes a safe *undo* possible, through a new entry in `TRANSITIONS` that only some roles may use.

+**2. Safe order intake from the point of sale.** Orders would arrive from the till and delivery platforms through `POST /orders`, which today is open and not retry-safe. A network timeout followed by a retry creates the same ticket twice, and the kitchen cooks it twice. I would require an API key per source and an `Idempotency-Key` header: the server stores the result of the first request for each key and returns it for any retry, as [Stripe's API does](https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests) and as the [IETF draft](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-httpapi-idempotency-key-header/) standardises.

O spec trata disso em dois lugares: a seção 2 ("AI") e o item 5 da lista de seções do `DECISIONS.md`.

## 1. Seção AI do `DECISIONS.md`

> *"In `DECISIONS.md`, name one AI suggestion you kept and one you rejected or rewrote. Be specific: quote the idea, not the tool brand."*
>
> *(§12.1) "One AI suggestion you kept and one you rejected or rewrote. Quote the idea and explain your reasoning"*

Ou seja:
- **uma sugestão da IA que você aceitou** e **uma que você recusou ou reescreveu**;
- **citar a ideia** em si, não o nome da ferramenta ("o Claude sugeriu…" não serve);
- **explicar o porquê** de cada decisão.

O que escrevemos cumpre isso: as duas citações são literais, com o motivo de cada escolha, e o nome da ferramenta não aparece.

## 2. A pasta `ai-logs/`

> *"Include your AI chat logs in the repository. Create a folder called `ai-logs/` at the root and export **the full conversation history** from the tool you used (screenshots, markdown exports, or .json files — whatever your tool supports). We will not penalize you for wrong turns or failed attempts in the logs; we want to see **how you steered the tool, what you asked, and when you course-corrected**."*

Ou seja:
- uma pasta `ai-logs/` na raiz do repositório;
- com o **histórico completo** da conversa, não um resumo nem um trecho escolhido;
- o formato fica livre: prints, markdown ou `.json`, o que a ferramenta exportar;
- o objetivo é ver **como você conduziu a IA**: o que pediu e quando corrigiu o rumo. Erros e tentativas que não deram certo não contam contra.

## O que isso muda na minha recomendação

Como o spec diz **"full conversation history"**, só o `.md` filtrado que sugeri antes pode parecer incompleto. Então:

- **O `.jsonl` completo** (o export nativo do Claude Code, que é um formato JSON) é o que cumpre o spec ao pé da letra. Ele é obrigatório.
- **Um `.md` legível** gerado a partir dele é opcional, mas ajuda muito o avaliador. Ninguém vai ler 25 MB de JSON, e o `.md` deixa visíveis justamente os momentos em que você corrigiu a IA ("SIGA O SPEC", "não precisa dos números…", "NÃO PODE MOCAR TEMPO").

Esses momentos jogam a seu favor: o spec diz explicitamente que quer ver isso.

Um ponto para você saber antes: a mesma seção 1 do spec diz *"Time box: 4 hours, stop when you hit it"*, e o log completo mostra a duração real da sessão. Como você vai falar disso ao vivo, deixo como está. Só não dá para cortar do log sem descumprir o "full".

Gero o `ai-logs/` com o `.jsonl` completo e o `.md` legível?

content.text:
A collection está pronta e testada: `postman/kitchen-queue.postman_collection.json`.

**O que tem dentro.** São 24 requisições em 5 pastas, cada uma com testes do Postman:

| Pasta | Requisições |
|---|---|
| **1. Queue** | fila ativa (o teste confere a ordem por score), `?status=received`, `?status=preparing`, filtro inválido → 400, `/ready`, `/finished` |
| **2. Create** | cria um pedido e salva o id em `{{orderId}}`; cria outro e salva em `{{cancelOrderId}}`; `items` vazio, item de menu inexistente, vários campos inválidos de uma vez, JSON quebrado |
| **3. Lifecycle** | start → **start de novo (409)** → cancelar em preparo (409) → ready → pickup → start num pedido finalizado (409) |
| **4. Cancel** | pular etapa (409) → cancelar → cancelar de novo (409) |
| **5. Errors** | id inexistente (404), id inválido `abc` (400), rota inexistente (404) |

A URL base fica na variável `{{baseUrl}}` (`http://localhost:4000`).

**Como usar:** no Postman, *Import* → selecione o arquivo. Rode a collection inteira, em ordem, pelo *Collection Runner*: a pasta "Create" salva os ids que "Lifecycle" e "Cancel" usam.

**Verificação:** rodei a collection inteira contra a API real com o Newman, o executor de linha de comando do Postman. Passaram as 24 requisições e as 44 asserções. A primeira tentativa falhou porque o **Docker Desktop estava desligado** (o computador deve ter reiniciado). Eu o liguei e subi o Postgres, que agora está rodando. No fim rodei `db:setup`, então a demo voltou ao estado inicial.

A pasta `postman/` está no repositório. Quer que eu adicione uma linha no README, na seção de API, apontando para ela? Ou prefere deixar a collection só para uso seu, fora do commit?

## O que estava sem sentido

1. **Uma encomenda distante no topo.** A regra de espera do SPEC conta desde a hora do pedido. Uma encomenda feita 90 min antes, para retirar mais tarde, ganhava pontos máximos de espera e passava na frente de um delivery VIP prestes a vencer.
2. **A cozinha parecia ignorar o próprio ranking.** Havia pedidos em preparo que, no momento em que começaram, **não eram** o primeiro da fila.
3. **Os tempos não batiam**: um prato de 16 min estava "em preparo" havia 12 min, ao lado de uma mesa com 70 min de preparo pela frente.

## Como ficou

Usei uma regra simples: **todo pedido em preparo começou no momento em que era o primeiro da fila**. Não confiei no olho: rodei o código real da nota para cada momento e confirmei.

| # | Pedido | Nota | Leitura de quem está na cozinha |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Grace**, VIP, retirada em 9 min | 95 | já em preparo há 25 min, quase pronto |
| 2 | **Ben**, mesa grande (2 ribeyes + salmão) | 90 | em preparo há 30 min; é a mesa que espera há mais tempo |
| 3 | **Alice**, mesa esperando há 1 h 25 | 75 | **Next up**: a mesa mais antiga ainda não iniciada |
| 4 | **Felix**, delivery VIP em 19 min | 60 | empata com Emma e vence porque tem horário prometido |
| 5 | **Emma**, mesa há 30 min | 60 | |
| 6–7 | **Chloe e David**, encomendas para a noite | 25 | por último, como devem estar |

Bônus: os números dos pedidos (#1, #2, #3…) agora coincidem com a posição na fila, o que facilita a leitura.

## O SPEC continua respeitado em tudo
- **A fórmula (§5.1) e o desempate (§5.2) não mudaram nada.**
- O seed continua demonstrando todos os itens da §9.5: os dois limites máximos (o Ben demonstra os dois), os empates desempatados pelo `promised_at`, os três tipos, VIP e não VIP, e received, preparing e ready.
- **Os empates se mantêm por pelo menos 45 min**, então a demonstração não se desfaz durante o painel. Depois disso, o "Next up" passa naturalmente para o Felix, cujo prazo vence. É o que um restaurante esperaria.

## Verificação
- 130 testes passando, linter limpo.
- **Todas as verificações do navegador passaram**, incluindo o "Next up" pulando para o próximo quando o primeiro começa a ser preparado.
